Why not?
I will give you one reason why I do not
think it is desirable for the House -to sit on Saturday. I can see the possibility-I will not say the probability, but certainly the possibility-of millions of estimates being rushed through on Saturday night when there is a very slim attendance. I am just as anxious as anyone else to see the session come to a close next week, but merely for the sake of attaining that end I will not agree to something that may result in passing hastily through the House millions of dollars of estimates. It would be better to sit until next summer than do that.
Mr. G; R. GEARY (South Toronto):	I
wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards). At the moment there is a most important bill before the railway committee. Many of us would like to attend that committee but we desire to be in the House at the same time, and this frantic endteavour to clean up business at any cost, in order to get away at a certain fixed date, is not conducive to sound legislation or to the proper conservation of the interests of the people. We should not allow ourselves to be stampeded into rushing through legislation and passing estimates without adequate consideration merely because we desire to prorogue at a given date. There is, I know, a strong desire on the part of everyone to get away as soon as possible; we all share that feeling. Nevertheless, it is a ridiculous spectacle for this country to witness this House, after a session of but two months conducted in an easy manner, passing legislation hurriedly and disposing of the business without full consideration because suddenly, a few days before prorogation, we decide to clean up everything. The House and the committees are meeting simultaneously and hon. members are anxious to be in both places, but this is impossible. If we desired to do so, we might clean up all the business of the House in a couple of days, and I do not know why the country should not conclude that parliament ought to be able to convene at the first of any month, have its committees and the House meet at eleven o'clock each day, sitting simultaneously, adjourning at two o'clock in the morning and thus dispose of the business of the country at the end of the same month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: It is like the investment by banks in the stocks of another bank. That is what it gets down to. It is really doubtful as to whether or not life insurance companies should own shares in another life insurance company. It has been held always to be a bad policy for banks to own shares in a competing bank. I only mention the matter because I was not able to be in the committee when the bill was being considered. I think this involves a matter of extremely doubtful policy.

An explanation was given
before the committee which seemed to me fairly satisfactory. That was that it enabled Canadian companies to take an interest in the shares of a British company, for instance, and thereby secure business through that British company in which they owned shares.
This applies not only to British companies but to foreign companies.

If it. were a British or United States company I do not think the same objection would apply. Perhaps "foreign" is too broad, but it must be a foreign company which is licensed to do business in Canada. In the committee I listened to the discussion and to the arguments which were brought forward by the representatives of the insurance companies, and it seemed to me that they were at present labouring under a disability which this legislation might help to remove. That was my impression from listening to the long discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is pointed out that in Great Britain fire insurance companies are permitted to invest in, or carry as assets in their statements, the stock of other fire insurance companies. In the United States this practice has, as a rule, not been permitted, but in some states of the union such an investment is allowed. I think the committee considered this provision very carefully and we might well allow it to pass.

On this point the committee, I think, was unanimous. The situation is that a British or a foreign company has, with respect to Canadian business, an advantage over the position that a Canadian company has in the reverse case, and the committee was inclined, therefore, to put a Canadian company on the same basis as a British or foreign company. I may say that the legislation was asked for especially by two. of the oldest Canadian companies-one, the British American, operating, I think, for ninety-three years, and the other, the Western, operating for something like seventy-eight. It was pointed out to the committee that if either the British or the Western companies desired to exercise the privileges that British and foreign companies have it would be difficult for them to do so. They were required to wind up any company which they might acquire by control and to do business in roundabout ways through an underwriters' agency. The committee, in a word, thought that all companies licensed to do business in Canada should be on the same basis.

I listened with a very
great deal of interest to what the minister said and I do not at all agree with him because this permits a Canadian company to do, not what the hon. member from St. Lawrence-St. George and my hon. friend from Toronto have said, but to hold shares in any other Canadian company. Now that means just what has been condemned so strongly heretofore in this House-one insurance company acquiring shares in another company. The result is that you have all the evils that have been denounced from time to time with respect to control and directorate. If it were limited to British or foreign companies I could quite understand the point made by the hon. gentleman, and I am familiar with the cases referred to; but when you empower Canadian companies to acquire shares in other Canadian companies you open the door to a condition which should not prevail with respect to insurance even though it be limited to fire insurance.

speechtext:
The House resumed from April 1 consideration in committee of Bill No. 259, to amend the Post Office Act

Hon. Mr. Veniot. -Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Has the Postmaster General received protests against this?

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Would the minister be good enough to indicate the intention of the administration with respect to them?

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
When this bill was in committee before, I gave an explanation of it. Since then I understand that many telegrams have been received from what is known as the smaller daily newspaper associations in several parts of Canada. There are about twenty-five interested in sending out these telegrams. They are not opposing a reduction of the rate, but they are asking that the reduction be deferred until they have an opportune of laying before the government their claim for the establishment of what is known as a zone system, that is basing the rates on newspapers on the distances of their circulation. They further state:
We favour a zone system whereby a great saving would be effected to the Post Office Department. It is fairest all round.
In 1920 when this act was being amended increasing the rate to one and one-half cents per pound in regard to certain classes of printed matter, the same delegation appeared and asked that the zone system be considered. It was very fully considered in 1920, and the decision reached was that such a system would not be practical in Canada owing to our sparse population. Since receiving this telegram and knowing that a number had been sent to other hon. members, I went fully into the matter with officials of my department and we still stand by the result of the decision reached in 1920.
These gentlemen who are protesting state that they are to meet in convention on the 4th and 5th of May. If when they meet at that time they will present any stronger

Post Office Act
reasons for the establishment of a zone system than they presented in 1920, the department will take their representations into consideration, and if their claim is a just one and if we can put it into force without affecting too much the revenues of the department, we will prepare something in the form of an amendment to this legislation and bring it before parliament next session. I see no reason why the bill as it is now before the House should not pass because it will not affect adversely the parties who are objecting. No matter what investigation may be made at the present time along the line of establishing a zone system, it would be absolutely impracticable in Canada. They have no such zone system generally throughout the United States. They have a zone system in the congested districts, but there are no sections of Canada so greatly congested in population that the zone system would work advantageously here.
I may say further that I have received a letter approving of this action that the Postmaster General is about to take. It is addressed to the hon. Minister of Finance from the Canadian National Newspapers and Periodicals Association, affiliated with the Canadian Press Association, and says:
On behalf of the members of the Agricultural Press Association of Canada, the Magazine Publishers' Association of Canada, and the Business Newspapers' Association of Canada, all of which are affiliated with this association, I wish to express our appreciation of this proposed legislation, which presages a welcome measure of financial relief and leads us to hope that when the whole case of the periodical publishers has been dealt with by the government. we will have reached a parity of production costs with our foreign competitors.
Since they refer to their foreign competitors, let me say for the information of the House that I am of the opinion that something should be done to-shall I say-protect our publishers in Canada-

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: That is a good word.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: -to protect our publishers from the influx of American newspapers and American periodicals Which are to-day flooding the whole country. Since this bill was introduced, I have taken up this very matter with the various officials in the different branches concerned with newspaper postage and circulation, and during the recess a thorough investigation will :be made with a view to devising some scheme by which we can give greater protection to our newspapers and periodicals in competition with American publications.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that the
bulk of American publications do not come into Canada through the mails, but by express, over which the Post Office Department has no control at all?

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I am not in a position to
say yes or no in answer to that question, because I have only begun an investigation into this matter, but should they come into the country in that way, of course, it might be difficult for us to regulate them. I do know, however, that a very, very large quantity comes through the mails.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I have mentioned this
matter before, but I think the opportunity is good again to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that these Sunday and Saturday papers published in the United States and coming in here are largely advertising mediums, and not newspapers a.t all in the real sense of the word. For instance, a newspaper with fifty pages will probably carry about forty pages of nothing but advertising matter. Why should not the government of Canada receive a revenue from that advertising? If you do not want to penalize the literature that comes into this country, why not put a tax on the advertising carried by these newspapers, because for the most part they carry nothing else but advertising matter, which is circulated throughout this country to the detriment of Canadian manufacturers and Canadian industries, and helps to foster American ideas throughout the country in the households and wherever these newspapers go. If we cannot prevent the introduction of this literature, we ought at least to tax this advertising scheme, because three-fourths, if not seven-eighths of the whole thing is advertising pure and simple. This matter has been brought up several times before, and I hope the Minister of Finance in conjunction with the Postmaster General will see that a revenue is brought into the exchequer by placing a tax on the advertising columns of these papers.
A movement is on foot in the United States at the present time to reduce the size of these papers, because it is well known that the advertisers do not get the benefit from this advertising that they think they should get, for the ordinary man when he picks up a newspaper of forty or fifty or sixty pages has not the courage or the time to scan through the whole business, and he will simply look at the sporting or literary section or any other section in which he is interested, and throw the rest away. It is a waste of paper and a waste of time, and so far as we
Post Office Act

here are concerned it is a waste of revenue. I think in this sixtieth year of confederation the Minister of Finance and the Postmaster General would be well advised to get a revenue at least from this influx of American publications, if we can get nothing else. It would be another step in fostering a Canadian spirit in Canada, because we would not then be flooded by the ideas and ideals which come in here from another country, some of them very acceptable to this country, but a great part of them, I am sorry to say, should not be accepted by us.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: I do not wish to take the time of the committee but I would suggest that the Minister of Customs at the present time has it entirely within his discretion, by giving a proper definition to certain items of the tariff, to place a tax on all magazines which bring advertising matter into this country. I think if he will look carefully into that and take the legal advice of his officers, he will find that the matter is entirely in his discretion at the present time.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
In common with other
members of parliament I have received several telegrams in connection with this bill, one from Mr. J. R. Burnett, of the Charlottetown Guardian, on behalf of about thirty newspapers.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Twenty-five.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I thought it was more; twenty-five, or whatever the number may be. This seems to be a rather important matter when we find such a number of newspapers throughout the country interested in it. I will take the liberty of reading just a short extract from this telegram:
The present bill is an attempt by some big daily to steal a march on the others. Nothing will be lost by delaying till the dailies have an opportunity of expressing their opinion, and we would urge you and all members to oppose its passage this session.
I can see no reason why there should be any hurry about this particular bill, and I was glad to hear the minister say that if the bill does pass, he will hear the representations of these men -who will be gathered together in Toronto on that particular date mentioned. I merely take up time at this moment to present the case of the smaller dailies who appear to think they are going to be oppressed by this legislation.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Proportionately most of
those small dailies mentioned in the telegram will benefit more than the larger newspapers because the circulation of some of them is so small and they now come within the forty-mile zone provision

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: And they will not get any benefit from a change because they go free in the forty-mile zone.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Yes, so they really have no reason to complain, and they ought to know it. They are not paying to-day, some of them, and they will only pay provided their subscription runs to 2,500, and circulates beyond the forty-mile zone. They have that forty-mile zone now, but they want us to establish zones all over the Dominion. It cannot be done, according to the information I have from our experts, and therefore they should not ask to delay this bill.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
But the dailies are not within the forty-mile zone provision.
Mr.-VENIOT: Some of them are and some of them are not. I do not want to mention names, but I have a case right here with which I am quite familiar. This daily has only 750 subscribers, and the paper does not go outside of a 20-mile zone. They are given everything free, and yet they are complaining.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: I was going to suggest to the minister that perhaps he might do this. He might provide that this section shall come into force on proclamation so that he could have an opportunity-because he would have power under the Postal Act to regulate the matter; I do not know whether he could do that reasonably or not-but it would give him the opportunity of hearing the representations by those interested on the 1st of May, and the act could be brought into force by the beginning of July in any event.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Supposing we did that.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Then they get nothing.
But if you did agree, under the regulations of the department, I think you would have power to make those provisions afterwards.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: No, I looked into that very carefully.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Then that answers it.
The only other alternative would be to let the matter go over for a whole year.
There is another point that I think the right hon. Prime Minister might consider in connection with this matter. The formation of national sentiment is influenced by factors which are sometimes conscious and sometimes unconscious to the people themselves. When my friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) made his observations with respect to advertisements. I thought it might afford me an opportunity to say something that has been in my mind for a long time. Take a magazine such as that mentioned by my friend from

Post Office Act
Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) the other evening, it costs at least nine cents and is sold for five cents on the street. It is perfectly clear that the advertising it contains is so very lucrative that its publishers can afford to sell their production at a half of what the white paper costs. Let us look at it. It advertises goods manufactured in the United States at much lower retail prices than we can even produce them. That is, with a population of 110,000,000 their mass production enables them to advertise various goods that the Canadian housewife uses every day at a retail price less than they can be manufactured in Canada, much less sold.
This brings about a certain amount of distrust of our whole economic system and of the conduct of national affairs. It also does much to form a public opinion antagonistic to the very country in which we live. The effect of reading those advertisements of motor cars, washing machines, canned goods and various other commodities-I give only two or three illustrations, others will occur to hon. gentlemen as I proceed-the effect of reading those advertisements-and everybody reads them-especially on the minds of young people, is to make them ask: What is wrong with Canada that I should! have to pay so much more for these things than the price at which they are sold in the United States? The result is that public opinion is being formed unconsciously and the whole national sentiment of the (country is being more or less wrongly influenced, and this in turn injuriously affects the creation of that strong feeling of Canadianism that we are all so anxious to encourage.
I do urge that it is within the power of the Minister of Customs, as my friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) says, to deal with the matter, and I am confident that the co-operation of the Minister of Customs and the Postmaster General, with the Minister of Finance strongly aiding them, would bring about such results as in my judgment would have a beneficial effect not only on the revenue-I am not thinking of that so much at the moment-but, more important still, on the body politic by preventing the circulation of such magazines containing advertisements which are detrimental to Canadian sentiment, for they reflect upon the ability of Canadians with our limited population and vast area to produce goods on terms to compete successfully with those produced in the United States having the advantage of mass production and an enormous consuming market. We have talked about this for so many years that I suggest the time has come for action, and this
action will, I think, commend itself to every hon. gentleman, especially after having listened to the very able statement made the other day by my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: It is exceedingly gratifying, Mr. Chairman to find that at last we have one minister who appreciates the serious handicaps under which this great industry is suffering in this country.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I am a newspaper man,
although I am not in the business now.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: The owner of that paper with 750 circulation?

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: No, I got sold on that.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
What the minister proposes, although not all that is necessary in view of the competition from the other side, will be some slight relief for the publishers of this country; and since he has found it good policy to make this proposal I submit there should be no objection to it from any part of the House. Our tariff at the present time is 15 cents a pound on advertising matter. We allow magazines to be imported containing 240 pages, 150 pages being advertising matter on which no duty whatever is paid. Those magazines are not in the real sense of the word literary productions. If they depended upon their literary contents for profit they could not live at all. They are primarily advertising sheets. Those 150 pages of advertising are just 150 pages of printed matter that is admitted under the tariff of 15 cents a pound.
Now, it has been contended by the officials of the Customs department that they would find it very difficult, if not impossible, to separate the advertising from the reading matter and impose the tax. Of course, that is an entirely superficial view because in the United States they do separate the two; the postal rates there are higher for advertising than for literary pages. So what is done there ought to be done here. But let us get down to the two items of the tariff that are applicable. Item 184 provides for a duty of 25 per cent on just such publications as are coming in here. Another item imposes a duitv on any literature of this kind that is unbound. Now, I should like the House to pay attention to this. By an arbitrary ruling of the Customs department made many years ago these magazines are said to be unbound. During the debate on the budget I produced one such magazine of sixteen different sections. How it can be argued that that is unbound is beyond my comprehension. Such
Post Office Act

an argument could not be maintained before any tribunal. If the items now in the tariff schedule were fairly interpreted according to their language, and properly applied, there would be a tariff of 25 per cent on ail these foreign publications. I submit that that is not enough, but at least it would be something worth while and would have this effect: it would discourage certain publishers who have undertaken extensive subscription campaigns in Canada. The publishers of one particular magazine have set themselves an objective of 500,000 copies a week in this country, and have engaged some of our best canvassers to assist them. Since they started the campaign they have increased their circulation 50 per cent. Now, even if the tariff were only 25 per cent, it would discourage those enterprises, and it would foe a warning to their promoters that the time may come-as I hope it will-when they will have to bear a heavier impost.
I have argued with (the Finance minister now for four or five years to get a little relief, and I am delighted this morning to discover that at least one minister, and a minister in a position to do something, is seized of the urgent necessity and the undoubted justice of giving this much consideration to the publishing interests of the Dominion. I have in mind the publisher of a certain daily newspaper which does not go into the mail to the extent of more than a few thousand, but all of whose circulation, which is a large one, is distributed by carrier in the city of publication. I find that particular publisher very active in trying to prevent this bill going through. The telegram read'by my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island cites a number of other papers which are practically in the same position. They are not paying anything, and they do not want anyone else to get relief, simply because they are not- personally interested. That is a very narrow and selfish attitude for them to take. On broad., national grounds this bill ought to go through, and there should be no objection from any quarter.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
As regards the suggestion that there is an attempt on the part of some big dailies to steal a march, let me say that there is no big daily newspaper in Canada that has ever approached me in this matter.
I have been a newspaper man myself for more than thirty years, although I am out of the business now, and I know from experience the burden that is being carried by the newspaper fraternity of Canada to-day. That burden I am attempting to some extent to relieve. When I laid the matter before the

government they accepted the policy which I am now submitting to the committee, and I want to assure hon. gentlemen that so far as I am concerned absolutely no influence' has been brought to bear on the part of any big dailies. What I am doing now I am doing on my own initiative because, from an experience of some thirty-five years in the newspaper business, I feel that this measure of relief is due at the present time.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: What does the minister think of the zone system asked for in the telegram?

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
It is impracticable in
Canada, and I might as well make the statement now for the benefit of our friends so that when they meet in convention they may advance the strongest arguments possible to convince the department that they are right and we are wrong.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
This is not a party question, and I may therefore venture to remind the committee that at one time I was Postmaster-General and consequently am very much interested in the whole subject. I will not refer to the number of newspapers and reviews published in the United States which are daily and weekly invading Canada with their mass of advertising matter that comes in practically free to the disadvantage of Canadian publications. That is not the phase of the situation to which I desire to direct the attention of hon. members.
I want to refer the Postmaster-General (Mr. Veniot)-and I am in earnest in this, for I speak the mind of a large number of good citizens of Canada-ito the very strong exception which is being taken to the large number of pornographic papers, magazines and other periodicals sold in our large cities, such as Montreal and Toronto. I do not know so much about Toronto where I visit two or three times a year. Certainly, however, Montreal and even Ottawa are being disgraced to-day by the sale of these pornographic papers, which are being read by our young men and women and even children. These newspapers are on sale at every street corner in our principal cities, and w'hile I know that the Postmaster-General is not primarily responsible for their obnoxious presence I do think that he and the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) might get together and devise some drastic means of stemming the flood into Canada of this mass of deleterious reading matter. Every police magistrate in the -city of Montreal, in the light of investigations that have been held, has de-

Post Office Act
dared that convictions, especially of juvenile delinquents, can invariably be traced to the reading in the first instance of newspapers and other publications carrying pornographic news and pictures. Even in France, which as everybody knows is as free as any country can be, there is at the present time a decided movement against the purveying of literature of this sort. The other day I was interested to read that a member of the clergy in the city of Paris had passed from one street to another there, destroying as he went along all the pornographic advertising matter which came to his notice. He was brought to the court and I admired his speech in defence of what he had done. "Could I", he asked, "allow poisonous matter to find its way into the hands of children, young boys and girls, and refrain from destroying it in the interests of their morals and for the good of society?" The judge in pronouncing sentence upon the accused practically admitted that he was right, but unfortunately the purist could not take the law into his hands and so he was obliged to convict him. He fined the priest one franc. With the franc at its present value, the fine was purely nominal.
I hope the Postmaster General and the Minister of Customs will' deal with this matter in a drastic way. We must protect our youth and prevent this literature from invading our cities and finding its way into our homes. Some years ago, when Postmaster General, I negotiated with the authorities at Washington a modest treaty which to a certain degree kept this literature out of Canada, and concurrently with that treaty I made arrangements with the British Postmaster General to the same elnd. A preference was given to papers and reviews published in Great Britain; this was known as the British intellectual preference. I followed very closely the effect of that legislation, not only in Washington and London but in Canada as well, and I was agreeably surprised after a little while to observe that in the large centres newspapers and reviews of high moral character were being sold to the people. Just before the war, however, this arrangement with Great Britain was discontinued for financial reasons. I would ask the Postmaster General to study the question to see whether it may not be possible to restore that arrangement, which I can assure him was quite beneficial.
A large number of immigrants from the British Isles are settling in western Canada. They are far away from neighbours, and of course they like to read the news from home. Shall we allow cheap dime novels and pornographic papers, published in some of the western United States cities like Chicago, to cross the boundary and become the principal reading matter of these new settlers? I think these settlers would appreciate news from home, which would help keep sacred the ideals to which they were born and bred. I am only offering these remarks to the House, Mr. Chairman, in order to facilitate the task of the Postmaster General, who I hope will become a great reformer at least in the matter of Canadian literature and the ideals of the Canadian press. It is a sad spectacle to see, even here in this good city of Ottawa which is to become a great capital, tabloid papers being sold at every corner.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: There seems to be general agreement with respect to this bill, and I think we are all aware of the difficulties with which our publishers have to contend in order to compete with the publishers of the United States. We are also aware of the tremendous effect of literature on the public mind, and I think we all agree that there should be developed a real Canadian spirit, sentiment and outlook, and that in the creation of these national sentiments literature plays a part equal to that of any other influence. Personally I am glad that some recognition is being given to the difficulties of our publishers. There have been several suggestions made as to how they might be assisted; one is that a tariff might be placed upon American publications, while the other suggestion is that a tariff reduction should be made on the machinery, accessories and so forth used in the publishing business. I have no solution of my own; I do not know which of those two ways would be the better, but the present proposal does not raise the question of tariffs. This bill will bring about a slight reduction in postal rates, which I feel sure will be appreciated by the publishing business generally in Canada. I do not quite appreciate the point raised with respect to smaller publications; while they may not receive any direct benefit from this bill, I fail to see where they will receive any injury and I think the bill should'pass.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I am not opposed to the
bill, but there seems to be a disposition to inject into the discussion the question of the tariff and the question of customs duties. The whole matter of the tariff on magazines is at present before the Tariff Advisory Board, which I presume to be the proper place for the consideration of such a question. I have no objection to the board considering it, but I would object to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Post Office Act

Robb) raising the tariff on magazines until such time as the case had been heard by the tariff board, and the report and evidence submitted to the House.
With regard to salacious matter in our magazines, I have no doubt that it is very objectionable, but the only way to deal with that matter is by police regulations. If these regulations are not sufficiently strict, make them so, and in that way eliminate these magazines from our street corners. That is a much better way than putting a tariff on these publications, or excluding them. If they have a criminally immoral tendency let the police deal with them. There is a section in the Criminal Code by means of which magazines of this kind may be dealt with, and if the law does not cover this matter amend the law in that respect.
With regard to the influence of American magazines upon the families of our country, I rather think we are hedging our Canadian boys and girls about with so much paternalism that they will not be allowed to choose for themselves; I do not see why our young people should not read a good many of these magazines without having their ideals affected. I have raised several boys and I have never tried to exclude American magazines from their reading matter; I think perhaps they have even gone a little too far in their ideas of Canadian independence. If we attempt to restrict their reading matter in this way, I think we will be going too far, because I believe our Canadian boys and girfs come of a stock which shows a great deal of initiative, and they should ibe allowed to exercise their own discretion.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I rise to call the attention of the committee to an incident which has just occurred and which I think should be noted. The presiding officer of this House has seen fit to address a few remarks to this committee and I think we should take note of the innovation. I do not know that- I draw attention to the fact by way of protest at all, because the remarks made by His Honour were very useful to the discussion and very elevating in their tendency, but the question is whether the Speaker of this House has the right to discuss any matters before the House. If His Honour has that right in this case, I do not' see why he should not have the right to discuss any matter which comes before parliament. I noticed in his remarks that he expressed the desire to facilitate the efforts of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). No doubt' that is a very laudable desire, but there are members of this House who do not think this measure is

proper, and I doubt if it is within the right of the Speaker to express an opinion upon any matter before the House. His Honour the Speaker on more than one occasion has laid down the doctrine pronounced by a celebrated Speaker in England in these words:
May it please Your Majesty, I have neither eyes to see, nor tongue to speak, in this place but as the House is pleased t >
direct me, whose servant I am here-
I think we should note the innovation, and I do not say this by way of protest against anything His Honour said, because no one has a higher respect for the Speaker of this House than I have. While a Deputy Speaker is allowed to take part in debates in the House on non^controversial matters, I have never in my experience heard a Speaker of the House take part in any proceeding except when the estimates of the House of Commons were before the committee. I think we should take note of this proceeding, because in the future it may become a precedent and I think the Speaker in his own interest should1 be prevented from taking part in the debates of this House. The rule says he shall not take part in the debates of the House, but whether or not that applies to committee I am not going to say at the moment.

subtopic: POSTAGE RATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Having been at one time
Speaker of this House I am somewhat familiar with the practice as to the restrictions upon the occupant of the chair. We are all at one on the point involved that the Speaker should never take part in any debate in the House except for the purpose of explaining his own estimates. That is a well known rule of parliament. But I know that the House is disposed this morning to overlook the course pursued by His Honour in view of the motives which animated him. Mr. Speaker spoke for the youth of the country on high moral grounds, and to further the development of that sound Canadian sentiment which we are all striving to see realized in this golden jubilee year of the Dominion. I am sure that the leader of the opposition, as he himself has said, has no intention of blaming the Speaker, and I quite agree with him that it would be out of place for His Honour to take part in our discussions having reference to matters of ordinary, everyday occurrence. In the present case, however, His Honour spoke from his experience as Postmaster General, and with the laudable purpose of promoting the circulation in Canada of a larger number of British periodicals. Because, after all, we are part and parcel of the British Empire. We have greater interest in promoting the circulation

Post Office Act
of British periodicals in Canada than we have in promoting the circulation of periodicals from the adjoining repuhlic. I am responsible, to a certain extent, for having initiated the discussion upon this particular phase of thie matter. But toy purpose in doing so was not to prevent the entrance into Canada of American publications as such but to try and stem the flooding of this country with American advertising, which is purely a business matter.	As the hon. member for
St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. C'ahan) has pointed out, the Minister of Customs has power to exact from the publishers duties on the advertising matter ini American newspapers that come into Canada. In this connection may I say that I was a commissioner for the city of Montreal for a number of years, and in that city a medical man or professional man of any kind cannot hang out his shingle, nor can a business man exhibit a trading sign, without obtaining permission from the municipality and paying a fee therefor. Now why should this Dominion be flooded, not through the mails but through the railway service, with huge piles of American periodicals which are nothing less than vehicles for advertising-advertising which does not appear in our own newspapers, which is not of a character congenial to us, and which is not favourable to the maintenance of Canadian ideals. It was on that ground that I spoke at an earlier stage of the proceedings, and I am sure that if His Honour went a step further than he should have done, he was influenced by the motive that we should further, on, moral ground, and to the greatest extent in our power, the creation of a sound, virile Canadian sentiment, particularly among the youth of this country. We have only to look around us to' see what is happening in this country. Those hon. members who are interested in the subject may read a speech, delivered in another place this session, by the chairman of the divorce committee, in which he alludes to certain ominous signs of the times. Over 1,200 divorces, for example, granted in one year. In this matter, I am afraid, we are imitating the example of the United States, where one marriage out of seven was dissolved last year. We must be on our guard as to the effect upon our young people of certain kinds of moving pictures and illustrated books, some of which are denounced even in the United States and by churches and religious organizations of all kinds. Over there these organizations have been quite free in condemnation of papers and periodicals that should not be allowed to circulate in a decent, re-32649-129
spectable country. Some of these publications are a disgrace, they should not be allowed to enter a respectable home, and we should be on our guard lest they contaminate the morals of our boys and girls, the future citizens of our country. I feel that it is the bounden duty of the government of Canada to act in this matter, and that in any action they may take along this line they will be backed up by public opinion. We had a sad experience in Montreal in the opening days of the present year. I allude to what happened at the Laurier Palace theatre when, owing to a violation of the law, seventy-eight young children became victims of exploitation through the medium of a moving picture show. It was an event which attracted the attention of the whole world, and even His Majesty the King sent his condolences to the city of Montreal. It is true this is largely a provincial matter. But the films which are introduced into these moving pictures come through the customs and for that reason it is possible for the Minister of Customs to take some remedial action. I am sure there is no greater work we can do for this country than to purify its atmosphere, maintain a high standard of morals, and protect our young people, so that we may be able to build up in Canada a great, a prosperous and a moral nation.

I am glad
to hear that statement from the Prime Minister. He will appreciate, no one more readily than he, that where there is a difference of opinion, as is likely to exist regarding this or any other expenditure, a wrong impression might easily be conveyed. I welcome his statement so far as he is concerned in relation to the approach of the roads to his summer residence. I think he has taken the proper stand; it is one which I certainly appreciate and which I believe the country will approve. I say I am glad that he has taken that position because, whatever we may think of the advisability of carrying on this work on the other side of the river, I think it is wise, as the Prime Minister will agree with me, that no false impression should be created that the work is being done with any ulterior motive or that any particular person shall benefit thereby and, most of all, the Prime Minister of the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Above everyone else, in connection with an expenditure of this kind, he should be free from any possible imputation that the money was being used for the express benefit of the property which belongs to him. I am glad therefore to have this assurance from him.
I realize that I am not very much of a diplomat; I am not built along diplomatic lines. My method of diplomacy is to go straight at a thing and not around a corner. That is the only kind of diplomacy I understand. I make my own statements direct, and I want equally direct statements from others. By following that course we can arrive at the
truth of matters and act accordingly. Now for my own part I do not like spending money across the river; it is going far afield. However, I may be wrong in that and the judgment of the House will prevail.

It is a little out of place
for the Ottawa Improvement Commission to go across the river to build driveways or create parks. I understand the park is not contemplated in this bill. It seems to me that where the money should be spent is close to the parliament buildings. There are thousands of Canadians coming to Ottawa who will never see the driveways, for during six months of the year the driveways cannot be used. The money should be spent in beautifying Ottawa and especially in the vicinity of these buildings. The buildings along Wellington street are certainly not an agreeable sight. First of all, Wellington street should be improved, and I hope the Minister of Finance, or whoever will have charge of the matter, will see to it that most of the money will be spent in improvements of this description and not in the construction of driveways outside the capital. We might also have a little bit spent in cleaning up the streets at this time of year. Some of the streets of Ottawa are a disgrace to any capital. Sand and dirt are allowed to accumulate on the top of snowbanks, and after the snow in the country has been gone for a month you can find great piles of ice and mud in the city. This condition exists about this time of year along .the streets within a block of the parliament buildings and it is a disgrace to the capital. The improvement commission should do something to beautify that .part of the city close to the parliament buildings.

I was not in the House
yesterday when the matter was discussed but to me it seems fitting that the parliament of Canada should set aside an amount yearly for beautifying the district around the capital. As regards cleaning the streets of Ottawa, surely the city council should attend to that. It should form no part of a great comprehensive scheme of this kind. With reference to the driveways, I am heartily in sympathy with the proposal. The federal district of Ottawa will not end at the Ottawa river. Ottawa is approached from the other side of the river as well as from this side, and if we are going into the scheme we should have long vision and enter upon it with a comprehensive plan. As regards the suggestion of the hon. member for Frontena.c-Addin.gton, it would be most unfortunate if, because the Prime Minister happened to be interested in

that particular section, the Ottawa Improvement Commision should be deterred from making a driveway even past Kingsmere should they determine this to be the best course. It would be most unfortunate, I say, for us to allow any such petty prejudice to interfere with the work of the commission. I hope that the suggestion of the leader of the opposition regarding the commission will be accepted, and that when the work is undertaken it will be done in such a manner as will produce something that will arouse the pride of all the people of Canada.

I have been in this House long enough to see hon. gentlemen change their views with a change of geographical position in the chamber. The hon. gentleman from Lisgar is one of them. He was severe in his criticisms when he occupied a place in the southeast corner of the House, but now he is on the other side his views have been wonderfully modified. He is now willing to build roads, from Halifax to Vancouver almost, if it meets with the approval of his present leader, the Prime Minister. The hon. gentleman speaks very learnedly, with his head in the clouds, about long vision. Well, it seems to me that we shall require something more than that before we get through with this proposition: we shall require some of the long green to meet incidental expenses. The hon. member is perfectly justified in taking the position he does if he wants to beautify Ottawa all the way from this point to the city of Montreal-
Oh no.

-and westerly some sixty or seventy miles, or to any extent the government may consider within the environs of Ottawa. It all depends upon what the Prime Minister and the government say. If the Prime Minister says that the radius of the environs shall be ten or twelve miles to take in Kingsmere, very well; if the Prime Minister shifts his residence fifty-miles away and says that the environs extend that distance, the hon. member says, "AH right; make your roads long enough to take in whatever place you want to improve. We must beautify Ottawa, and Ottawa is to extend one- hundred miles if necessary." I commend the hon. gentleman on his very marked change of attitude since he eat on this side of the House.
No change whatever.
He is becoming very tractable indeed.

[Mr. brown.J

There is no need for any party whip where the hon. member for Lisgar is; there is no need for even a handle to the whip. All they need do. is hold it up and the hon. member for Lisgar will respond; every time they whistle they will not need a whip at all, yet he poses as a Liberal Progressive. Where does the Progressive come in? Once it was Progressive; now it is Liberal Progressive, but the Progressive is gradually dwindling away and he may as well drop it altogether.

I will soon have the same
honour as the hon. member for Label'le (Mr Bourassa).
You can put yourself in that class if you want to, but I hope to God I never will.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and the United Grain Growers are the only subjects on which the hon. member can make a speech.

The hon. gentleman has changed so often that I would not be surprised if he put himself in the same class with the hon. member for Labelle; changes come very easily to him.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that we have a certain amount of responsibility in connection with beautifying Ottawa, but in this as in other cases which I mentioned yesterday there is a disposition to spend money wholesale which in my judgment should be guarded against. What are the obligations of Ottawa in connection with this matter? Ottawa has no obligations at all. Do they receive any benefit through the fact that the seat of government is here? Look at the beautiful drives in Ottawa south; a few years ago, before the government began to spend money in beautifying the city, these drives were a series of frog ponds. What did the city get out of those beautiful drives? There are a number of splendid residences which never would have been there at all if it had not been for this expenditure. I think Ottawa is having it pretty easy; I think every government we have had has treated Ottawa pretty generously. I do not expect anyone from Ottawa to agree with that statement, because it would not be human nature; they will take all they can get and look for more; you can depend upon that every time. I do think, however, that the time has arrived when we should adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) and create a federal district to take

Federal District Commission
in the city of Ottawa, as is the case at Washington. If we are going to keep up the whole city, let us make it a federal district, and the sooner the better.

The hon. member for
Macleod (Mr. Coote) referred to the streets of Ottawa. The condition of the streets depends entirely upon the civic administration, and I agree with him that in the spring the streets of this city are in a deplorable condition. During the rest of the year and especially in the summer Ottawa is one of the cleanest cities on the North American continent, but they do not seem to have a proper appreciation of the removal of snow. If we are going to undertake to keep the streets of Ottawa clean in the spring there is only one way to do it; declare this a federal district taking in Hull, if you will, and appoint a commission to govern the city. I cannot help repeating that that seems to me the logical thing to do now, instead of waiting for sixteen years, over which period it is proposed to stretch this expenditure. That might and should, in my judgment, disfranchise the citizens of Ottawa and prevent them from voting in the federal elections, and to my mind that would be one .of the best things that could happen any government. The way the Amalgamated Civil Servants hold the gun to the head of every federal government is well known to every member of this House; if a member does not know that, he has not been here very long. Let us do what they have done in the United States, create this a federal district and appoint a commission to govern the city. The citizens should pay a reasonable municipal tax, and this parliament would then undertake all responsibility for the beautification and improvement of the city. I submit to my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) that he should get up and advocate such a commission, and the immediate creation of a federal district.
It is too late in the session.

Will my hon. friend do
it next session?

I am sorry I
cannot agree rvith my namesake, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). We must always remember that in beautifying this city we are beautifying the capital of Canada. We are proud of Ottawa; no city in Canada is more beautifully located, surrounded as this city is on all sides by scenic beauty. This bill provides that the drives for a short distance out of the city may be improved. But some hon. gentlemen think
it is unnecessary to spend money anywhere except in Ottawa. We know that hundreds and thousands of people from other countries visit Canada every year, and since Ottawa is the capital city, naturally it is the place everyone wants to visit. We want these visitors to leave Ottawa with a favourable impression because if they are pleased with this city they will be pleased with the country as well.
I do not think this bill needs any defence; this improvement commission was conceived by Sir Wilfrid Laurier many years ago, and after years of residence in Ottawa I can now say as a representative of the city that the commission has accomplished wonders. Today we are asked to support a bill increasing the scope of its activities and creating a new federal commission with an increased number of commissioners and an increased grant. I think everyone on both sides of the House should agree that it is of the utmost importance that this money should be spent in beautifying not only Ottawa but the country surrounding it as well.

Mr. Chairman, there are just two suggestions I would like to offer the Prime Minister with respect to this matter, which has been discussed so frequently that I have no intention of taking up much of the time of the House. I desire to point out the deep interest of all citizens of Canada in beautifying the capital, but on the other hand it seems to me there should be a fixed radius within which the operations of the commission would be carried on, say within ten miles or fifteen miles of the city. I think it is .an invitation to bring pressure to bear upon the commission from time to time, if the radius is not defined, and it would be greatly to the advantage of the commission if they had a fixed limit within which their operations should be carried on. It seems to me that that would relieve them from unnecessary pressure from many quarters.
My next suggestion is merely that which was made by the leader of the opposition and approved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I think the Prime Minister might well assure the House that in the selection of this commission partisan politics would be forgotten and an effort would be made as indeed has been the case in the past to secure the services of public spirited, high minded gentlemen, of whom there are so many in this community, desirous of rendering public service to the community and to the Dominion by serving upon that com-
Federal District Commission

mission. They should not be altogether men of one political faith, although probably from necessity, having regard to the frailty of human nature, the chairman would be a supporter of the administration of the day. I think an assurance of that character would make it easier for the country to accept these proposals as being in the interests of the country rather than intended to be a political move in any way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I be
permitted to reply to my hon. friend's last point first. He mentioned that the chairman would be of the politics of the party in power. I may say that when the previous Liberal administration came into office we found that the position of chairman of the commission was held by a very strong Conservative. I took the view, and it was shared by my colleagues, that as he was a public spirited, high-minded gentleman who was serving the city well, we would make no change in the chairmanship, and during the whole time that my administration remained in office, Mr. Fraser, a well known Conservative, remained the chairman of the commission. It was not until Mr. Fraser resigned that a new appointment was made. I think that in the meantime hon. gentlemen opposite had been in office. When we came into office again the position became vacant, through Mr. Fraser's resignation, and we were very fortunate in being able to secure Mr. Thomas Ahearn as chairman of the commission, a gentleman who I am sure everyone in this House and in this country recognizes as second to none as an able business executive and a very public spirited citizen, a gentleman who will give to the capital great service in that position, a service it should be remembered that he is rendering gratuitously. On the present commission there are a number of Conservatives. The intention is to continue the present personnel in that regard, to make no change, and I can assure the House that when additional appointments are made the greatest care will be taken to select gentlemen who will be recognized as well qualified for the position and meriting recognition because of the place which they hold in the community as public spirited citizens.
As to fixing a limit of radius, I would have no hesitancy myself in doing that. Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved the second reading of Bill No. 234, to amend the Pension Act.

It is with considerable hesitation that I rise at this stage of the session, Mr. Speaker, to make extended remarks upon any subject, and
particularly to make a criticism of the administration of a department. This subject is one which has been before parliament every year since the war. For the past two years there have been serious problems confronting the returned men which have not been dealt with, despite the fact that representations have been made by the soldier organizations from one end of the country to the other that serious injustices are being suffered mainly because, in their view, the Pension Act requires amendment. So far as I am concerned.
I may say that I share their view that the Pension Act requires amendment, and I say further, and I emphasize this, I believe that many pensions are being denied to applicants because of an improper administration of the Pension Act. Regarding amendments, the Canadian Legion met during the present year at Winnipeg, presided over by General Sir Percy Lake, and they made certain recommendations, which were in turn placed before the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. There has been a very considerable period of time within which to consider those recommendations, but there has been no action taken, and in view of those recommendations I must say that I was astonished to read in Hansard an answer to this effect by the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment in reply to a question asked by the member for Westmorland:
Present pension legislation provides pensions for all disabilities "attributable to or incurred during military service" and for "disabilities resulting from injury or disease or the aggravation thereof incurred during military service.* No ex-soldier who is so disabled is denied pension.
If that is a correct statement of the facts, Mr. Speaker, I would ask why did we in 1924, for instance, introduce and pass amendments to the Pension Act-amendments which have not vet* become law? Did not the government and parliament consider in that year that those amendments were necessary to do justice to the situation that existed then, and which still exists? Otherwise, why did parliament unanimously pass those amendments? If the minister has not had time to give proper consideration to the recommendations of the Canadian Legion, why is it not possible for him to reintroduce at this session of parliament the amendments to the Pension Act which the government has considered, and which this parliament actually passed unanimously, but which have not yet become law?
I propose now to leave the question of legislation to other speakers, and to devote myself to a statement in regard to the ad-

It has taken me considerably over one year to make up my mind that the only course which I can honestly follow is to bring to the attention of parliament the present situation which exists in this department. That agreement called for the payment of $509 at the rate of $30 a month from January, 1915. Some difficulty arose as to the amount and it was determined by the Department of Defence that, though the mother was entitled to separation allowance as the soldier's dependent, the wife should 'be given assigned pay of $20 per month; and at the time of the death of the man the wife had received all but $40 of the total amount due under the separation agreement. I did not call on you for the purpose of having a personal argument but simply to impress upon you the aspects of this case, which are favourable to the applicant, and to render you any assistance I could by reference to certain legal authorities and, at the same time, to emphasize the urgency of the case in view of my early departure from Ottaw'a and the many years that have elapsed since same was first brought to the notice of your board.
On the 11th of January last I wrote the secretary of your board requesting permission to examine the file herein. On May 13th, I forwarded two additional affidavits herein, and, also, stated that I was anxious to present the case to the commissioners at a full board meeting, but before doing so desired the opportunity to examine the evidence contained in the file so as to prepare myself.
In a letter from your secretary dated May 31st the 7tli June was fixed for hearing. At the same time the board refused to permit me to examine the evidence on file. Subsequent to the receipt of that letter I advised the secretary of the impossibility of proceeding with my presentation unless permitted to see the evidence on the file, and more particularly the evidence which I had placed there myself. I was advised that the board refused to alter its decision, and I, therefore, placed the matter before the minister, who produced the file for me about one hour before my appointment with the full board on June 7th. I attended the meeting of the board on that date, and presented my views fully to two of the commissioners, yourself being absent, though in the city.
I might add that I have had no explanation of your failure to keep that appointment. On the same day, and subsequent to the interview, I wrote you personally and requested that the case might be finally considered during that week. To date I have had no akcnowledgment from you of that letter.
Recently I was requested by a representative of your board to prepare a summary of my views on the case for further consideration. Although I had already spent approximately three hours with the board on the 7th instant, explaining my views, I undertook the preparation of this summary and have spent several days analyzing the facts and investigating the law, and on the 24th instant I forwarded this summary to the board marked "urgent", and requested the earliest possible consideration.
In my interview with you to-day I found you had not yet given any consideration to the summary and advised me that it would be impossible to do so either to-day or to-morrow'. I again emphasized my strong desire that the matter be finally settled before the House prorogued.
I do not propose to go into further details at the moment, but I once more request that this matter be given prompt consideration, and that if my conclusions are not understood or agreed with I be given opportunity of appearing before the full board for the purpose of elaborating thereon.

In the opinion of the board the question of whether the widow of the deceased soldier was or was not entitled to pension depends upon whether they lived together as man and wife subsequent to the execution of the agreement.
Now on June 30th I took this same question up with the Acting Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and requested him as minister of that department to arrange a hearing at which he should be present. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw your attention to what has been done. I have heard nothing in reference to this matter. If a decision has been reached it has not been communicated to me, neither has it been communicated to the applicant. I found for the first time yesterday that an investigation was conducted, and I will recount the nature of that investigation.
There is on the file a letter dated July 12, 1926, written to the director of the administration of the Department of Soliders' Civil Re-establishment in Vancouver, with specific instructions contained in it to interview certain people and to make a report. Although I live in Vancouver and was vitally interested in securing any information for the board and in cooperating with them in securing the true facts from 1915 to date, I never heard that the investigation was being carried on. I was not communicated with.
One of the people whom the director was instructed to interview was the widow's solicitor who has placed on file a letter and a hearsay declaration, a declaration in which he states that they told him they had lived together. That was not direct evidence at all and they were to interview him only because of this fact:
Mr. Lucas should be interviewed and informed that General Clark has quoted him to the board as stating that he, Mr. Lucas, does not remember anything about _ the case. A signed statement should be obtained from him as to whether or not he now' has reason to doubt the accuracy of his affidavit and, if so, the grounds upon which such reason is based.
I did interview the solicitor and he did tell me that he remembered nothing about the case. I see nothing extraordinary about that because his declaration is dated in 1917 and
my interview with him was in 1924, or seven years afterwards. If he did not refresh his memory by looking up the files and taking considerable time over the matter, he certainly would not be likely to remember much about it. There is nothing extraordinary about that. He did so tell me and I so stated to the board. I will however accept his evidence at its face value. It is hearsay evidence; even if everything that he states is true, it is not evidence at all.
The other people to be interviewed were the mother of the widow and the wife of a contractor. This latter woman, by the way, had made the statement that the widow had lived in her apartment house and that she always thought she was a widow; that she had never seen any man with her there. But her husband apparently had made a statement to the investigator of this department that Aylett, the deceased, had frequently or at some time visited the widow there. So far as I can see there is no confirmation of that by sworn testimony.
These were the three who were to be interviewed, but there were no instructions given to investigate the accuracy of the other affidavits which are on this file and which are probably ten in number, although I have not counted them. No instructions were given to interview those who indicated that they were favourable to the case of the mother. Apparently only those who had given unfavourable evidence previously were to be interviewed. Let me quote one or two paragraphs from these statements. This is a letter by Nellie M. Wood, dated 7th August, 1926, in which she stated:
I explained to Mrs. Aylett that the only knowledge I had respecting Mrs. Harriet Aylett-
That is the widow.
-was that at one time she did reside with her mother at Irving court, and that as I never saw her husband or any man about the premises at any time, I naturally presumed she -was a widow, to which statement I still adhere.
Then this declaration is filed:
I, Sarah A. Cusack, of the city of Vancouver, .... do solemnly declare that I have been the manageress of Shaughnessy lodge, Vancouver, B.C., since May, 1914.
This was one of the places where this man was supposed to have resided with his wife after the separation agreement. She continues :
I have a very clear recollection of Mrs. Harriet Aylett, residing in this apartment house, together with her mother and sister. I

Pension Act-Mr. Arthurs

am only too pleased to verify the fact that there is no question whatever, that Mrs. Harriet Aylett was at all times a strictly moral woman and her character was always above reproach.
She was at all times a perfect lady, but always very sad and quiet.
There is no suggestion there that the husband was ever around. I notice that in several of the reports of the investigators this man is referred to as a weak character, and it is stated that probably because he was a weak character he would be likely to write just as affectionate letters to his mother as to his wife. The facts are that no evidence has been produced from the widow that she ever received a letter from her husband while he was in France, but there are copies of very affectionate letters to his mother and these suggestions from the investigators that this man whom they had never seen was a weak character are entirely uncalled for. Before this man proceeded to France, he was one of one hundred chosen out of eighteen thousand as a guard of honour for His Majesty the King. He paid the supreme sacrifice, being killed in action in France while serving his country. He made a will in favour of his mother, a will recognized by the Department of National Defence. He wrote to his mother and apparently did not write to his wife. With this evidence as it appears on the file, I am forced to the conclusion that these facts have never been properly presented to the Board of Pension Commissioners, or they could not have arrived at the conclusion that:
There appears to be no doubt that the agreement of separation was rendered null and void by the subsequent cohabitation of the soldier and his wife.
We are surely all determined to see that justice is done, and if there are cases that we as members of parliament or as private citizens are prepared to present to the Board of Pension Commissioners, we should be given an opportunity to do so. By the way a proper presentation in detail in this case would in all probability take some hours, but I am satisfied it would disclose that the summaries of evidence prepared for the Board of Pension Commissioners to pass judgment upon were prepared by men who do not understand the analyzing of facts for presentation to a judicial body.
This file .discloses to me a situation which in my opinion calls for a very careful investigation. I was prepared to cooperate with the minister and carry out that investigation, with the minister alone present, so that he could hear my presentation of this oase in detail, and thereby avoid the publicity infMr. Clark.]
volved by bringing before this House the situation which exists, and which is in my opinion extremely serious from the point of view of applicants for pensions in this country. I shall at all times be prepared, Mr. Speaker, and I think this file will bear me out in that, to give any amount of time to elaborate on this case, or to go out and collect additional evidence for the pensions board, so that the board will have before them 'the full evidence. I urge as strongly as I can that the time has come for a full investigation into this department, and if an investigation is not made between now and next session I would suggest that an investigation might be made before a parliamentary committee both on questions of administration and as regards the amendments that are required to this act.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say some words with reference to this bill, and particularly with reference to the general question of administration of the Pension Act. To me it is a great disappointment that in this the first session of a new parliament steps have not been taken by the government to bring down early in the session legislation for which there is the most pressing need, not only in regard to the actual cases of extreme hardship which are known to the department, but also in regard to the many cases which are not before the department and the details of which are little known. The present Minister of Soldiery' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King) has only lately taken that post, and in my experience with him he has done everything possible to facilitate the meritorious and deserving cases, but the government generally seems to be very lethargic or indifferent in the matter of grappling with this question and taking hold of the problems which confront the returned soldiers. I myself in 1923 introduced legislation concerning amendments to the Pension Act, embodying ideas that were common throughout the country at that time and have been emphasized time and again since. During the last two years we have had no legislation of any consequence relating to pension matters. In 1925 there were some minor amendments only, and in 1926 there were none. Now we find the returned soldier organizations presenting a memorandum con-
