taining in the most complete manner their suggestions based on actual experience. If the government could not have presented the proposed amendments to the House this year, I think they could at least have carried on an investigation which would have advanced a solution of these problems. Just to indicate how widespread is this demand on the part of the soldiers for action I might mention that only a' couple of hours ago I received a wire from the Collingwood branch of the Canadian Legion in these words:
Have wired Dr. King registering protest against postponement of pensions and insurance legislation.	-
I stated on the orders of the day the other day, and I wish to repeat now, that in my judgment it would be a great mistake for this parliament to hurry the business of the session to a close at an early date and neglect to attend to these vital matters which should receive attention. I wish to repeat the assertion I made then, and I think I can properly do so because this is practically the first occasion on which I have addressed the House this session. I wish to repeat what I said the other day, that the men who are suffering from the ills of war, who spent their time in France in the service of the citizenship of this country and of its institutions, can now properly call upon members of parliament to spend a few days or a few weeks, or months if necessary, to deal with these urgent questions which so vitally affected them, and1 it is to be regretted that the apathetic and unsympathetic attitude which in my judgment is characteristic of the pension board seems to^have permeated government circles.
Some of these matters which the Canadian Legion have brought forward-I will not gn over them in detail-are of urgent importance. They relate to the soldier himself, to the widow, to the children, to the orphan, and to the other dependents of the soldier. They cover technicalities in the Pension Act which have made its administration contrary both to the will of parliament and the people of Canada and I do not think it would require such elaborate consideration as the minister suggests to take care of some of these more urgent matters under the present bill. I say this because these questions have to my knowledge been considered for the last four years, evidence with respect to them has been presented to parliamentary committees by soldier institutions, and there are men in the department who thoroughly understand them and realize there are technical defects which require no consideration to correct.
Pension Act-Mr. Ladner

Let me refer for a moment to a particular case which the minister has been kind enough to offer to take care of under the existing law. It is the case of James Frew. James Frew is entitled to a pension, and is now an inmate of a military hospital. The pension board, as so frequently happens, turned down his application. Under the statute he must make his appeal through the soldiers' advocate within thirty days of the pension board's judgment, and James Frew accordingly instructed that official to proceed with his appeal within a few days after receiving notice from the pension board of their refusal of his application. Through an error in the office of the soldiers' advocate, not due to the official himself, the statutory period of thirty days passed by and no appeal was made. The error was discovered' and the appeal proceeded with. The Federal Appeal Board decided, as it so often does, upon the inherent merits of the claim and awarded a pension to James Frew. The pension board thereupon exalted itself to the position of a court of appeal over the Federal Appeal Board and maintained that as the appeal was not proceeded with within the statutory period, therefore the Federal Appeal Board was wrong in its decision and the pension should not be paid. The poor man is in a serious state of health in the hospital, and he is very seriously handicapped by the lack of a pension.
I took the case up with the department, and in this respect I want to commend the minister for his kind offer to remedy the situation. Personally he is not to blame at all. I outlined all the facts to the deputy minister last year and proposed to him that there be put in the Pension Act a provision such as is to be found in the Supreme Court Act, vesting authority in the court to extend the statutory period of time in order that justice may be done. There is no discretion granted to the Board of Pension Commissioners and they are very dogmatic and dictatorial in administering the act. It would have been very simple for the department to advise the minister of this defect in the act and that the necessary power should be given to the federal appeal board to grant an extension of time for appealing or -taking other steps where good cause could be shown for the delay. But what happened? The pension board and the deputy minister refused categorically to make any suggestions for such an amendment. Then I proposed that if they would intimate to me when amendments to the Pension Act were under consideration I would bring in my amendment as a private member, but they said they did not think any amendments

would be 'considered. There is an example of sticking fixedly by a decision irrespective of its injustice to the man who by the will of parliament and the Canadian people should receive a pension.
These and other cases in the administration of the act are evidences to me of a most unsympathetic attitude and confirm the charge which I have long made, and which I repeat now, that whenever there is a question in doubt the pension board, although they have all the necessary evidence to establish the applicant's claim, -throw the burden of proof upon the applicant-the very person who is without evidence. Against these things the soldier bodies of this country object. Indeed, if they were not law-abiding citizens in some cases they would be incited almost to revolt because of the flagrant injustice of which they are the victims.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are some other matters which should have been dealt with this session. The information is already in the department to enable the minister to come to a conclusion. Let us take, for example, the allowance to orphan children of thirty dollars per month. I refer to this because I have been asked by women's organizations connected with soldier bodies to bring it to the attention of parliament. To-day this allowance is quite inadequate for orphans reaching their teen age, because they then are more expensive to maintain than a grown person. It is suggested that the allowance should be increased to forty-five dollars per month. This of course means an increase in the pension allowance, but not to such an extent as to make it unreasonable for parliament to grant.
Let me refer to another point of administration. Under section 1 of the act dealing with the age limit on pension to ghildren it is provided:
No pension shall be paid to or in respect of a child who, if a hoy, is over the age of sixteen years or, if a girl, is over the age of seventeen years, except when such child and those responsible for its maintenance are without resources and the child is unable, owing to physical or mental deformity, to provide for its own maintenance, or where such child is following and is making satisfactory progress in a course of instruction approved by the commission, in which case the pension may be continued until such child has attained the age of twenty-one years.
I ask the House to bear with me for a moment because the interpretation of this section shows conclusively the unsympathetic attitude on the part of the officials in administering the act. The point to which I wish to direct attention is the extension of

time in the advanced stages of a child's education. I have under my hand what I believe is authoritative information that approximately 98 per cent of the applicants for extended pensions under this section are refused. If the father who provided for these children had not been killed overseas, if he had not made the supreme sacrifice, he would have been here to give them the necessary education. The department's refusal was based upon a ruling which differs from the interpretation which most of us would give to the law. According to them "satisfactory progress" does not mean what it naturally would to us; it refers to those who "show exceptional ability." In other words, there is a constant effort to limit and narrow the field within which claims may be made for pensions by those who are entitled to them.
There is another question, the facts regarding which are all in the department, which it would not take the government half an hour to make up their minds upon. I refer to the matter of burial, medical and hospital services to children and other dependents. The present pensions to dependents and orphans make no provision for grave emergencies and serious illness, hospital and burial expenses. Apparently the provision is designed to take care of the minimum normal requirements, but it seems to me that it should include such expenses as I have referred to. I mention these as some of the matters that ought to be considered.
I was not present if the minister made any statement in reply to a question I asked on the orders of the day a short while ago as to whether or not the time would be extended for returned soldiers' insurance. Was an answer given to that question?

Yes, on March
30, I think.

I do not approve of the
minister's decision, but that I suppose is a matter of difference in policy. I do commend the minister in coming to a definite decision instead of being altogether indifferent and leaving the matter in a more or less unsettled state as some of us have reason to know is done in regard to other things.
I want now to refer to two or three cases to illustrate the point I am making, that the department is unsympathetic and that their effort appears to be to avoid paying pensions rather than to favour the applicant in doubtful cases and thereby do justice. I refer first to the case of R. E. Worthington, which can best be stated by reference to a letter I have on file from this man. I quote:
To make a long drawn out story short, I was finally taken very seriously ill with an hemorrhage, gastric ulcer not a duodenal ulcer, as Ottawa thinks. The doctor was called in at 5 a.m. on November 17, 1924, and inside of half an hour I was in the operating table for a major operation at St. Paul's hospital, about six blocks away from where I live. I may say that I was not expected to live the day. However I ultimately recovered and asked for payment of the hospital account and the doctors' fees, including two special nurses. The account runs approximately $600 (only for hospital bills and M.D.'s.). I did not ask for pay and allowances of my rank (which is captain).
You will read from the enclosed letter that I should have applied for permission to the nearest military hospital. Now, Mr. Ladner, how in the world could I have had time to make such application when the whole thing was done in half and hour and in the middle of the night almost. Indeed, the attending physician said I would not reach the hospital alive, which was only a short distance away. It was a question of life and death which I think should be recognized by the medical authorities.	,
Now then supposing I had died on the way. It has been recognized and admitted in the enclosed letter that my illness was occasioned hy military service. In that case my wife would have claimed a pension for the rank of captain. Don't you think, that in such a crisis, coming on in a moment, one could not think of asking to be admitted to Shaughnessy hospital which is at least four miles from my home? Then again it is a question of getting a dying man to the nearest institution.
I communicated with the department in reference to this case and received the reply that the man ought to have applied to the nearest pension authority. If that had, been done the pension authority would undoubtedly have agreed to allow this doctor to do the operation, and the expenses would have been paid. I would point out however that the exigencies of the case were such as made it absolutely impossible for him to communicate with a pension authority. I want to be absolutely fair in these matters, especially as I know the officials experience great difficulty in administering their department. But I do not think that such treatment is fair, and the suggestion, conveyed in a letter to me, that the man knew a night or two before he was taken to hospital that there was something wrong with him, is not warranted. In the space of half an hour he was seized with this illness-this can be confirmed-and in a dying state he was rushed to the hospital. He had no time to think of formalities and technicalities. An hon. member suggests that he would not know the formalities. That is more than
Pension Act-Mr. Ladner

likely, but at any rate it is certain that he had no time to consider such things. Yet the department refuses to consider his case and reimburse him. That in my opinion, only confirms the statement that the department is unsympathetic, one might almost say heartless, in its attitude towards many of these splendid men who have suffered disabilities and illnesses in consequence of service overseas.
I want the minister to understand that in making these statements I have no intention whatever of indulging in a political speech. We are five years from an election, and in any case this matter is of great importance and far transcends the narrowness of partisan politics.
It may be to fulfil a political promise.

There is no reason why
the hon. gentleman should suspect me of following his own practice.
That is not my practice.
I live at another end of the continent.
Too bad for you.

No, on the contrary it is a good thing, in view of my hon. friend's idea of political morality.
I have two or three files full of cases such as the one I have cited. There are instances m which there is merely a misunderstanding of the intent of the law, but in a large number of cases there is revealed an indifference to the condition of these men and a desire to get out of paying the money to which they are entitled. Here is the case of John S. Hunter. The record number is 505,378, the pensioner's number being 136,439. This man was injured in the foot overseas and on discharge he claimed a pension and received it. He was in receipt of the pension for four or five years but one day he got a letter informing him that it would no longer be paid. The pension was finally reduced by half. However, the man made complaint, and the reply came that no remedy was forthcoming, for the reason that at the time of his enlistment, to quote the words of the letter, "there was a tendency to flat feet." On behalf of this man I v'rote pointing out that when the pension was first granted all the evidence, including his hospital sheet, was before the pension authorities just as it was when the pension was discontinued. Not a single change had taken place, either in fact or in evidence, to cause the pension board to withhold the pension or to reduce
[Mr, Ladner. 1
it. Why did they change their minds? Did it arise from a deliberate policy to cut down on pensions? Why did they pay this man and then, on the same evidence, with the same facts and the same medical sheet, suddenly decide he was not entitled to pension? That is exactly what happened, and I have never yet received an explanation except when one of the officials stated that they may have made a mistake in the first place in granting the pension. That is a typical case, and I appeal to hon. members whether or not the representative citizen of this country would not have decided that the pension board should have given the poor fellow the benefit of the doubt rather than take away his pension after he had received it under the same law and facts for four or five years.
I mention that as another indication of the lack of sympathy on the part of those administering the Pension Act; I had intended to refer to other cases, but I wish to expedite the 'business before the House. There is the case of Sarah Louisa Atkinson, which is equally meritorius; there is the case of James Parker Fee, whose disability was attributable to war service and was so established by the medical board, but whose pension was refused; there was the case of Charles Edward Bower, and as a matter of fact I suppose most hon. members have had a number of cases of people wdio claim pensions. I have endeavoured to select those cases which from my knowledge of the facts and my knowledge of the law have the weight of evidence in their favour, and in which the pension board had no right to refuse pensions.
The charge I make against the board is the same as that made in three previous years, and I find that a great many other hon. members now have the same viewpoint. It is my conviction that the board have been in office so long and are so tied u,p with red tape that they have become unsympathetic to these unfortunate Claimants and narrow in their interpretation of the law; and that they have tended to put the onus of proof more upon the applicants. The board seem to have an unwarranted desire to save as much money in pensions as it is possible to save. I realize that those are strong words, but if hon. members could read the heart-rending letters which I have received and could visualize the homes upset and lives distressingly disturbed; if hon. gentlemen could picture the little children who, instead of being educated as their fathers would have done had a kind Providence led them safely home, must now go to work at an early age, I think it would
