be found that the language is not too strong.
I have had widows and wives ill in health, broken in spirit and without work, come to my office in Vancouver for assistance in their claims but who have been refused pensions on the slightest and most unworthy technicalities. Many hon. members have had the same experience I am sure.

I do not think the hon. member was in his seat a few moments ago when I stated that in speaking of the Board of Pension Commissioners one must bear in mind that they have a double function; they are administrators in some respects and judges in others. The hon. gentleman is attributing unworthy motives to awards made by that board, and in so doing is reflecting upon the character of those judges, because that is what they are in certain respects.
I wish to conform to the rules of the House, but I am merely stating true facts of which I have personal knowledge. I do not wish to reflect upon the commission-
Or their motives?
I do not think I referred to their motives.
The hon. gentleman stated that they had refused pensions on most unworthy pretexts.

If I may repeat it, what I did say was that in the decisions given it has appeared as though the board were endeavouring to save money and to force the onus of proof upon the applicant more than was formerly done. I think that is a fair statement to be made by a member who is seeking to do his duty. I have no doubt there are many members who take the opposite view, and if so they are entitled to state their opinions as well. My real purpose in these remarks is this: I would like to see the government seriously take hold of the question of policy, and seriously consider the representations which have been made by the various soldier organizations. Let them consider the facts and suggestions, by which any reasonable man would be convinced. The case of James Frew, which I pointed out a few moments ago, is typical. Under the act there is no provision by which appeals can be made after thirty days, and there is no authority such as is given to courts to allow an extension of time where good reasons are shown. These are things for which there can be no excuse while one man rests under a disability and an injustice as is the case with hundreds at present.
I have nothing further to say on the question, but I do earnestly urge the government and the minister to take time between now and the next session of parliament to consider thoroughly all these questions and to have legislation ready at the beginning of the next session which will correct these clear defects and offer a solution to those other problems which may be a little more complicated. There may be some questions for which it is difficult to find a solution, but there are many on which a few minutes reflection or a glance of the eye will warrant decision and action. The government have a responsibility for not attending to this important matter this session, and they have a duty to look after it next session and make those changes the necessity for which is apparent to any reasonable and sensible government desiring to apply the pension as was intended and is now desired by the people of Canada.

It was not my intention to take any part in this debate until I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark), who I am sorry to see is not in his seat. His remarks, generally speaking, had reference to one particular case, and before this high court of parliament he tried a case which has been already tried by a tribunal duly appointed by this House. In French we say, "Un plaideur malchanceux a vingt-quatre heures pour maudire son juge." The hon. member for Burrard, instead of taking twenty-four hours in which to curse his judge, brought the whole case before this House. I listened to it very attentively, and it seems to be a very complicated matter. The Board of Pension Commissioners in their wisdom, having at their disposal investigating officers; having heard from the eloquent lips of the hon. member on several occasions, and having read from the even more eloquent pen of the hon. member the whole facts of the case, have decided against him. After listening to his remarks for some time it semed to me, though I have every sympathy for the widowed mother of the deceased soldier, that the hon. member for Burrard was rather more interested in the fact that his feelings were hurt than that the pension was withheld from the person to whom he makes reference; it seems to me to be more of a case of lese majeste than a case of a really deserving character.
After having listened to him for some time I heard him say that he was very much offended because, forsooth, Colonel Thompson after listening to him-
Pension Act-Mr. Po-iver

I rise to a point of order. That is an absolutely incorrect statement. I did not say that I was offended because Colonel Thompson did nothing. Furthermore, if I may make myself perfectly clear on the question on the point of privilege, I wish to say that my personal feelings have not been hurt at all. So far as I personally am concerned that phase of the matter has never entered into this case, and the record will show it. The record will show great forbearance on my part, a forbearance for over three years; and the only reason I have made the statement now is in the hope that I may bring this situation to the attention of the government and influence them to deal with it.

I have no objection to my hon. friend interrupting me for the purpose of making a correction, but he must not deliver a speech. Of course I accept the hon. gentleman s word, but X listened to the reading of a letter which he had addressed to the Board of Pension Commissioners on the day following, or some days following, this remarkable interview in which Colonel Thompson walked out-
. Mri- CLARK: The interview was only an incident.

-and I gathered from
listening to the letter that at the time my hon. friend wrote it he considered he had been offended.
And you concluded you would have been offended under like circumstances.

I think I would have been.
I do not blame my hon. friend. I have been offended and iby the very same persons, but I did not think it was necessary on that account to take the whole of the cases I had brought before the board and submit them to the House of Commons. The law enacted by my hon. friends opposite was brought into force for the specific purpose of taking the whole question of pensions out of politics. For that reason we have, I think, since the war, and even during the war, treated the question of pensions for returned soldiers almost as a non-political one. The Board of Pension Commissioners was formed, practically by common consent, into a judicial body. Their tenure of office was fixed at ten years, they were not to be removable except on the same grounds as those for

which a judge is impeached, and it is for that very reason I understand, Mr. Speaker, that you refuse to allow us to impute evil or improper motives to members of the board. I have thought on many occasions that it wasi my duty to rise in the House and declaim against certain members of the board. I have thought sometimes that their judgments were not sound. I might go even further in my characterization but Mr. Speaker, perhaps, would correct me. I have thought their judgments were not sound, not based on common -sense, but I do not think that this is the place in which to try cases wherein, in my judgment, they err.
Now let me follow my hon. friend from Burrard still further in his remarks. He says, undoubtedly without political bias, that my hon. friend the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King) should be at his disposal to go and meet the Board of Pension Commissioners. He says that when he has business with the board he has a right, in the name of the returned soldiers, to say to the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, "You come with me''.
Not at all.

If the hon. gentleman did
not say that I do not know what he meant.
Not at all.

He said it was the duty
of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment to be present when claims were made.

-Once more, Mr. Speaker, I
absolutely contradict the hon. gentleman. That is an incorrect statement. I did not say anything of the sort. I said that I appealed to the minister on the ground of a certain condition existing in the administration of his department.
That he should go.

That be should go and hear one particular case as it would clearly illustrate, as regards administration, the situation in all -cases. I would dot ask the minister to go in all cases, but simply in this particular case to illustrate the situation in r-egard to administration. That is all.

He asks the Minister of
Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment to go with him before the board. I-t was not right, it was wrong, it was unjust, when -my hon. friend the present minister did not go, but it was a

Pension Act-Mr. Power
very different matter when the acting minister, belonging to the party of my hon. friend himself, last June was not able to go, saying that he was too 'busy.
I did not criticize either.

If my hon. friend did not
criticize I do not know what he means.
I simply stated the facts.

I remember my hon. friend
waxing quite indignant and saying it was the duty of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment to appear before that board.
His duty to do what?
Saying that it was the duty of the Minister of Soldiers' Re-establishment to go with him before the board.
In all cases.

The hon. gentleman did not say in all cases, he was talking of this particular case. Now if the failure to do that aroused indignation in my hon. friend's mind because the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment now sitting here did not go. surely it should have aroused, far more indignation in the mind of my hon. friend when he was wounded in the house of his friends. Let me go further. The object of this law, as I said, was to take the matter of pensions out of politics. If you are to permit the minister, the man who controls this department, to appear and to assist at the sittings of this body you will cause the impression to go out-by implication, either directly
or indirectly-that the minister is influencing the decisions of the bo-ard. To that I object.
I think it has been decided by this parliament in its judgment that the minister should not interfere with pensions. Many a time my own constituents have written to me to say: You have influence with the minister, you support him, you are on his side of the House, ask him to go before the Board of Pension Commissioners with you, ask him to write to the pension board. Never since I have been a member of this House have I asked the minister to influence the Board of Pension Commissioners in any way, but let me say that many a time it would have done some good if they had been influenced in the right direction.
There was another remark made by my hon. friend to which I think we have a right to take exception. He accused the government of shameful neglect because they had not put into force certain recommendations of the pensions committee of 1924. Surely my hon. friend would remember that the bill passed by parliament on the recommendation of the pensions committee of 1924 was defeated not in the House of Commons but in another house.

I said it was passed
unanimously by this House.
He did good work.

I thank my hon. friend for
saying that. The minister is a great influence in this government. Does my hon. friend think he will not continue to wrork for the returned soldiers?
I think he will.

Does he think the minister
will not continue to work for those for whom he fought not only while he was in France but after he returned to Canada? It is unjust, unfair and highly improper, at this stage of the game when the war has been over for ten years, when for ten years we have allowed this matter to be dealt with outside of politics, for my hon. friends opposite to try to make political capital out of a few petty grievances.

I
fail to understand why the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has taken the stand which he has in this debate. I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark), and it w'as not my impression derived from anything he said that a partisan spirit actuated his remarks in any respect. He had a case which, to anyone who heard it, conveyed the impression that perhaps an injustice had been done. He used it as an example to call to the attention of this House and of the government the fact that it might be well for the government and the minister responsible to look into the workings of the pension board. I have no complaints of a specific nature to make; but one cannot be a representative of the people without hearing of cases in which, rightly or wrongly, the soldier or his dependent thinks the pension board has not done justice. These cases are so numerous that one is sometimes compelled to think there may be a general principle underlying them, and that the pension board, in the very patriotic desire to avoid any imposition upon the government, has perhaps stood so straight that it has leaned backwards.
I do not think the hon. member for Burrard was making any imputation of wrongdoing
on the part of the pension board. He was saying that the impression gathered generally from many instances in which soldiers had communicated with him-and I can assent to that from my experience-was that the pension board's mind was more directed to saving the money of the government than to taking care sympathetically of the soldiers who came before it.
The hon. member for Burrard instanced a case which comes dowrn to a very narrow point. There were two claimants for a pension, a widow and a mother who was dependent and with whom the soldier lived. There was a question of fact to be decided. The board decided in favour of the widow and against the mother. The widow has since died. I think it would be the part of generosity and sympathy for the soldier when there is no longer any dispute, not to cut off at the death of the widow, the pension as it had been awarded, but to continue it to the mother, there being then only one. applicant involved. That would have been a sympathetic way rightly or wrongly, of dealing with the matter. I am not prepared to say if that might have been done.
The hon. member for Burrard is pointing out to the minister that the feeling exists-[DOT] and I think he pointed out as kindly as he could-that the minister should keep more closely in touch with the operations of the board and the disposition of the many cases which come before it. In that I think the hon. member for Burrard was quite right. This is not a judicial board in the sense that it is dealing with litigants who are at arm's length. It is a body which is dealing with the claims of men who are prima facie entitled to recognition of their claims.
We have found men who were bad soldiers in the army; we have had poor men when they went into the army and poor men after they left. I am not saying that they are all perfect; but the great bulk of the men who served overseas and who make claims for pensions, are to be relied upon. They are men who should be treated with a great deal of consideration and sympathy and with the feeling that they are not out in the first place to get from the government anything to which they are not entitled. Rather they believe thoroughly in the claim they are making and they should be entitled to careful and sympathetic consideration. Therefore I hope the minister and the hon. member for Quebec South will not take from the remarks of the hon. member for Burrard the impression which the hon. member for Quebec South seems to
Pension Act-Mr. Geary

think is the correct one. The hon. member for Burrard has spoken for himself. As one who is interested in the matter I may speak for many on this side of the House who are in the same position as myself. We do not speak from any partisan spirit; the time has gone by for that. The Pension Act is the result of careful investigation. The Minister of National Defence is responsible for a good deal of it and entitled to a great deal of credit for what has been done. At the time he was not actively engaged in politics; he was an independent chairman of the commission; he put his heart into the work, and we think a good job was done. The work is not yet completed. The object, as I take it, of the hon. member for Burrard, as it is my object in making these remarks, is to point out to the minister that this judicial body, so called, which is not judicial in the sense that it is dealing with litigants who are at arm's length, is one that might be supervised by the minister, and that interest taken by the minister in the specific cases or in the general conduct of the board would be amply repaid by what he could learn from so doing.
In regard to the bill itself there is disappointment amongst the soldiers of this country over the action of the government in quite another direction. The Pension Act is a mass of almost unintelligible amendments. I mean that those who read the act, those who are concerned in it and are to benefit under it, are men who have not the capacity for disentangling from a mass of documents the points which may or may not affect them. It is so difficult, Mr. Speaker, to follow that act that I myself have given it up in despair many times. Through the kindness of the government last year I was given a complete copy of all amendments, but that did not make it much better. The time for consolidation, as I said last year, has more than arrived, and I had hoped that the act would have been consolidated by now. Added to that, the soldier organizations to-day are on a far better footing than they have ever been before. Previously there were conflicting groups and associations with conflicting interests, but these bodies have been welded more or less now into a smooth-working and harmonious association called the Legion, which represents properly the sentiments of the returned soldiers in this country. That Legion has a service bureau. It has men qualified to look into the questions which affect the returned soldiers, and that bureau, after looking very carefully into these different questions, made certain recommendations which in turn were submitted to and passed

by the various provincial commands and at last reached the general convention of the legion which was held, I believe, last summer.
In January of this year.

In January, then; and these recommendations were referred to a committee of the Legion, with a representative of the department present, I believe, and probably taking part in the discussion-no doubt sympathetically, because I do not ascribe to any official of the department, least of all to the minister, any lack of sympathy towards the returned soldiers. Before this committee the various recommendations were sifted out, and their work finally resulted in some thirty-eight or thirty-nine recommendations being codified into suggestions for the department to act upon. Those suggestions have been in the hands of the department for I should say one month now, but the Pension Act has not been consolidated, and none of those amendments has been embodied in amendments to the act now under discussion. I regret very much indeed, and regret in common with many of the commands, many members of the Legion, many posts of the Legion and many individual soldiers, that we are left without any action being taken this session in regard to these carefully thought out recommendations. That is a matter of great disappointment. I do not know that it would do any good to propose any of these recommendations by way of amendment. It would probably not pass the House, but it does seem to me that many of these amendments, vital in their intention and necessary to the proper and smooth working of the act, could be arranged and carried into the bill we have before us. I object strenuously to the interests of the soldiers in this matter of pensions being sacrificed to any desire on our part to close the business of the House at an early date. This matter should receive the attention of the House this session, and as far as the department can go in deciding what amendments are proper and should be made within the next day or two or within the next week, these amendments should be presented to us and embodied in this bill. I protest against the delay in looking after the suggestions of the returned soldiers, officially made and carefully thought out, and undoubtedly, in the main, suggestions which would be of great service to the department and of great help and assistance to the [DOT]soldiers who are entitled to a pension.

Pension Act-Mr. Evans

I would
'like to say a word, Mr. Speaker, in support of the contention of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). He related some instances of hardship amongst the returned soldiers who are seeking a pension, and I have several in mind of the same kind.
I have often thought that there was an unsympathetic attitude on the part of the department towards these men. Whether the law or the regulations are at fault, or whether the thing is general, I do not know, but I do know myself of quite a number of cases of soldiers who should be on the pension list but who cannot get on. I think a more sympathetic attitude is due these men who have once offered their lives to save this country.
I have in mind one young man who took his discharge as physically fit. He had some slight ailment at the time, simply a nodding of the head, and when he was advised to get on the pension list if possible, he said, " Oh no, I can make my way. I will get well as I go along." But instead of getting better he got steadily worse, and for the last year he has been in hospital, at the mercy of friends. He cannot get on the pension list.
I have had his case before the board, and it is now before the soldiers' representative in Saskatchewan, but there is very little hope that under the present laws and regulations he will be able to get on the pension list.
I know of another man who, with one leg missing; is still trying to make a living. He failed for over four years to get any help from the pension board. He has an artificial limb, but it does not fit very well and cannot be made to fit, and he cannot use it.
I do. hope that- the minister will take into consideration all these cases that are brought before him. I really think that a more sympathetic attitude is due to these men; in fact I have always contended that once a man has taken his life in his hands and faced death for his country, if he is incapacitated in any way his country owes him a living. I shall be glad to give the minister the names and numbers of these men if he desires them.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to unduly delay the House in the brief remarks I propose to make touching this very important question of soldiers' pension legislation. I should like to associate myself with those who have alreadv spoken in the debate in their
deep regret that the government has not seen fit to bring down this session amendments to returned soldiers' legislation. I understand that- representations were made to the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment *in March last by the Canadian Legion officials and that a promise by implication, if not a definite promise, was certainly given at the time that the recommendations for amending the Pension Act then made to the government by the returned soldiers' organizations would be dealt with this session.
We often hear the remark made in this House:	We want legislation with teeth
in it-something that will be effective to cope with a situation requiring drastic treatment. The other evening when amendments to the Customs Act were before the House the government withdrew a clause that had teeth in it. Now with respect to pension legislation we have on the statute books an act with so many teeth in it that it is altogether too vicious in its operation. In certain of the provinces liquor legislation has been enacted under which the accused must prove his innocence, and he has no right of appeal from a conviction. Under the administration of the Pension Act practically the same result follows. A man goes before the pension board or the federal appeal board and must establish beyond all question that he is entitled to a pension. He is not given the benefit of any doubt-that is not characteristic of British jurisprudence in ordinary cases, and we certainly should be more lenient in dealing with returned soldiers who sacrificed so much for this country than to any other class of citizens.
The Pension Act has not been amended since 1924.

That is to be
amended.
There is to be an amendment this session?

Yes.

Pension Act-Mr. Sanderson

I am glad to hear it. It disposes of that point. There are however a good many other cases similar to this where injustices to the returned soldiers demand immediate amendments to the Pension Act. These amendments should not be delayed. They do not involve anything intricate and the necessity for them is well known to the government. Surely they can be introduced this year. The minister ought to make some definite statement suggesting some concrete changes, so that we might know exactly the position of the government. Such a statement from him would be highly appreciated by the ex-service men's associations in Canada. Legislation along these lines is urgently needed and we are asking the government to reconsider their decision not to bring down any amendments other than the one just referred to by the minister.
With regard to appeals to the Federal Appeal Board, I would point out to the minister that in the first instance the appeal is heard, not so much on the merits of his case as on what appears in his file. If there is anything detrimental in the file it looms up larger than anything else. This trial on files has a tendency to work a grave injustice to the man appealing and there should be some regulation to dispense with that procedure, if not altogether, at least to such an extent as would minimize the injustice which the returned men now suffer on that account.
There is another point worth touching upon and that is with regard to cases of misconduct. No appeal is allowed in such cases. I am also informed that of all the cases that have been appealed from the Board of Pension Commissioners to the Federal Appeal Board only 28 per cent have been allowed. I should like to have the minister make some more definite statement than we have so far had with regard to what the government intends doing with reference to the Pension Act and to returned soldiers legislation generally. This subject is certainly of far-reaching importance. The present conditions are a source of hardship and uneasiness throughout the Dominion to returned soldiers and their dependents and to returned soldiers organizations, and the matter is one that calls for immediate attention on the part of this parliament. Comprehensive amendments should be brought in during the present session, and I would urge the minister once more to make a clear cut statement on the subject.

I listened , to the speech of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) before the House rose at six o'clock, as well as to the
remarks of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) and I agree with both hon. gentlemen, one on this side and one on the other. I am firmly convinced that a revision of the Pension Act with proper amendments is long overdue. It is true that certain amendments were made in 1925 but there is room for amendments this year. I very much regret that the minister has not seen fit to bring in some amendment to the act.
This question has many ramifications, and could be debated in this House at great length. Every hon. member of this House has had a great many claims put in his hands from returned soldiers and their dependents, and if I may say so I think perhaps the great difficulties the pension board have had to deal with have resulted from several causes. When the war was over and the troops were sent home and discharged from the different military districts, many of the returning soldiers were discharged without a medical examination of any kind. I do not altogether think that the military authorities were to blame for discharging these soldiers with no medical examination, because in many cases the men themselves were to blame; they wanted 'to get out of the army and resume civil life, but they should not have been permitted to take their discharge without a medical examination. At any rate, many of them were discharged without such an examination; they have gone back into civil life and many of them, together with some who were discharged after a thorough examination, have been seized with certain diseases, or certain defeats have become apparent, which can be traced directly back to the effects of the war, and it is a very difficult matter to establish this after a few years have elapsed.
I do not want to take up very much of the time of the House, but I would like to mention one or two cases which have come under my observation in my own riding. The first case is that of a man who was a medical officer overseas; he returned from the war and was discharged as medically fit. He went back to his profession and tried to carry on, but after a lapse of a few months pernicious anaemia settled in his system and he became seriously ill. I am not a medical man and I do not know very much about that disease, but I do know that he applied to the board for a pension and was absolutely turned down, because the pension board said his physical condition could not be traced back to his war service. He protested that that was not so, and some of his friends took up his cause and went back with it to the pension board

Pension Act-Mr. Sanderson
Perhaps I am a little ahead of my story; in
the interval this officer had to go to the expense and trouble of taking special treatment in the Toronto General Hospital. His earning power was gone and he was not in condition to practise his profession; he was left with very little money and was virtually fighting for his life at the time representations were made to the pension board that at least he should be put under observation and should receive a pension if entitled to one. He went not only to the Toronto General Hospital but also to the Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, where a specialist looked' him over. The specialist, I should say, was one of the most eminent doctors on this disease in the United States, and he certified after learning the history of the case that the condition could be traced back to the first inoculation the man had received when he entered the army. Several medical men in Toronto who examined him agreed in that view. It took us months and months to convince the pension board at Ottawa that this officer was entitled to a pension, and if it had not been for his friends who rallied to his support and gave freely of their time in placing his case before the authorities, that man would not be receiving a pension at all, simply because the Board of Pension Commissioners said his condition was not due to his war service. That was their first decision, but when further proof was offered that decision was reversed, and they said his condition could be traced back to the first inoculation he received when he entered the army.
That is one case, and I have another which, came under my observation, that of a boy from my home town, who enlisted and went overseas with my battalion. I know the history of that boy and the history of his parents and his family for years back. When he returned from overseas he was discharged from military district No. 2, which was the first mistake; he should have been discharged from military district No. 1, from which he had enlisted. For some reason or other, in the shuffle coming across from overseas, he landed in Toronto and was discharged without a medical examination. He returned to his home town and started in civil life, but in six months was stricken down with tuberculosis. After a long fight we 'had him sent to London for observation, where he died two weeks later. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that if he had received the care he should have when he was discharged from military district No. 2, he would have been taken for treatment, with the result that he would have been alive to-day. I will say, however, that after he

died we brought the matter before the Board of Pension Commissioners, who granted a pension to his father and mother, whose sole support he had been. My contention is that that boy should have been examined prior to his discharge; if that had been done he would have been under observation, and probably his life would have been saved.
I have still another case which I would like to mention, and I have in addition some letters which I received only a day or two ago. This is the case of a young married man who owned a farm in the riding which I have the honour to represent. He went overseas and was both gassed and wounded, receiving treatment first in France and later in England. Finally he came back and received his discharge. He went back to the farm and worked for a year or so and was then taken down with heart trouble. His case was so serious that the local doctor recommended that he sell his farm and give up farming, as he could no longer carry on. He has done that, and I am glad to say that now he is under observation in London.
I only mention these cases to illustrate .the fact that thousands of Canadian boys were discharged from 'the army as medically fit, and perhaps were -medically fit at that time, but through their war service and through the hardships they endured overseas their systems were so undermined that certain diseases have afflicted them which can be traced back directly to their war service. I claim that these men should get fair, generous treatment from the pension board, and that there should be no hesitancy when their cases are brought up; they should get prompt and careful attention. I have not very -much criticism to offer with regard to the Board of Pension Commissioners other than to say that the trouble with the staffs of the pension board and of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment is that there is still too -much military red tape and discipline, and not enough careful consideration. I know that many cases have been brought up where no claim exists. I do say, 'however, that every claim should -receive prompt, favourable and careful consideration, and that there should be no red tape at all in -this connection. Their claims should receive more consideration than any appeal or request that is made to any other department of this government.
There is just one other matter I want to speak of. I gathered -from the remarks of my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power)

Pension Act-Mr. Guthrie
that an hon. member opposite had stated that sometimes politics have crept in in connection with some of these claims. If I am wrong in that understanding I am open to correction.

If I may rise to a point of order I would say this: at that time only the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) and myself had spoken, and neither of us, directly or indirectly, referred to or indicated that there was such a thing. The hon. member is entirely mistaken. We tried to keep politics out of the question.

I am not referring to my hon. friend at all. I did not hear anything that he said, and I did not hear the hon. member for Quebec South even refer to him. But I did hear the hon. member for Quebec South refer to the hon. member for Burrard. I want to say that long before I entered political life I did what little I could for the returned men, irrespective' of their politics, and am still doing it. I never saw anything in the shape of politics obtrude itself into the administration of the Pension Act at Ottawa here, either under the Union government, the Conservative government or the Liberal government. But now the question has been raised I want the minister please to pay attention to what I am going to say and to take it into his serious consideration. I do not lay any charge myself because I have not the proof, and I would be loath to prefer any charge against any official unless I had absolute proof. But if one-half the stories that have been told to me, and told to other hon. members from western Ontario on this side, are true, politics did creep into the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment in the city of London, and military district No. 1, during the elections last September. If half the stories told about the manipulations of some of the officers and some of the nurses on the staff there are true, then the minister should make an investigation and find out whether there is any foundation for these rumours. I do not know that they have been brought directly to his attention, but I am bringing them to his notice now and suggesting that in military district No. 1 there is room for investigation with respect to charges of partisanship on the part of officers and nurses in that area.
Let me say again, Mr. Speaker, that I would have been mudh more pleased if the minister had brought in his amendments to the Pension Act this session, and if necessary prolonged the session by two, three or four days, or even a week, in order to deal with them, because I think there are thousands
of cases in Canada that deserve and demand prompt attention from the minister in charge of the department. The trouble is that as the years go on we are forgetting a lot of things about the war. We are forgetting the claims of the dependents of the men who went overseas and were killed, or the claims of the men who came back maimed for life. These are claims which should receive careful attention and be given just consideration at all times.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer just a word or two upon the second reading of this very important bill. May I say in regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) that he somewhat spoiled a very estimable speech with an insinuation against a body of very worthy men and women in the military district of London when he stated that while he knew nothing about the matter he had heard rumours for which he could not vouch, and at the same time insinuated that these officers and nurses were guilty of improper actions and improper conduct in the month of September last. Up till that point in his address-

As a point of order I should like to state to my hon. friend the
leader of the opposition that I did not make charges, but that rumours were so serious and so grave as to merit investigation. Douht-less the hon. member has heard these rumours also.

That is not a point of order, Mr. Speaker, and I will not be interrupted in this irregular way. I said, and I repeat it, that my hon. friend did not make charges. What he said was that he had no knowledge of these rumours. In that case he should not have made his insinuation. That is my point. Letting it go at that, I say that in my judgment, he spoiled what otherwise would have been a very estimable speech upon this important question.
Now I think the minister to-night and during the course of this afternoon has had it very forcibly brought to his attention that the time is ripe for action in regard to the present Pension Act. Almost annually since the war this House has deemed it necessary to amend the pension law. We in this country, happily for Canada, had little experience in pension legislation prior to the war. But since the Great war we have had an abundant experience, and in the judgment of this House it has been necessary almost every year to appoint committees to consider the whole situation and amend the law where amendments were pro-

Pension Act-Mr. Guthrie

per. The last occasion upon which a committee considered the pension legislation of this country and brought in amendments was 1925, I believe. Nothing was done in that respect during the last session. Now we have come to the closing days of the session of 1927, and at this very late period the government brings down a proposal to amend the pension law only by way of appointing two additional members to the appeal board. I think the only other clause in the bill provides for a quorum of that board. Since this session opened it has been drawn to the attention of the government and of the minister week after week that the present pension law is unsatisfactory in some respects and inadequate in others. Notwithstanding all the amendments of previous sessions and all the investigations of committees of this House which have inquired into the question, there are still loopholes in our legislation; it does not cover all the cases which require attention. These facts, I say, have been brought to the notice of the minister and of the government week after week during the present session. The minister himself has informed the House that he has had requests from soldiers' organizations, I think he said to the number of over thirty, asking for remedial legislation in regard to pension matters. I think he said that his time was too fully occupied to take the matter up, or he had not time to consider these various applications.
No, that was not the statement I made.
Some excuse of that kind-
No excuse.

The minister can put me right when he speaks on this question later. At all events the fact remains that here, in the dying days of the session, the only thing which the government brings forward is a proposal to increase the number of officials; they offer no remedy whatever for the grievances of those soldiers who have been denied pensions under the law as it exists to-day. I do not propose to give instances, although I could, many of them in my own riding; and I do not lay any blame upon the pension board or upon the appeal board. What I blame is the inadequacy of our present law. I do not intend to cite cases, because sufficient have been cited to-night to show the necessity of doing something in regard to the Pension At-, and doing it this session. I do not think the government can successfully plead any excuse in this matter, because it has been brought to their attention too often during the present session. But here we are

in the last days of the session with no relief offered to the sufferers and no remedy proposed. One trouble with the present bill is that it is too strict in its language and too circumscribed in its application. It is almost in the nature of penal legislation. The board says that the language of the act must be construed strictly-and they may as a matter of law be right in that decision-and that they are unable to deal with many cases with which they would like to deal.
The Pension Act is in the nature of remedial legislation if ever remedial legislation was passed in this House. It should be elastic. Discretion should be given to the board. All legitimate applications should be permitted. The board in its inquiries should be given a liberty which it has not now. These matters have been drawn to the attention of the gov-erment time and time again by soldiers' organizations in Canada. The Canadian legion has passed resolutions on the subject; every member in this House, I assume, has, like myself, received copies of these recommendations, and yet the government has not moved a hand this session to relieve the situation.
We have an intimation from the minister at this late date-the first I heard of it was to-night-that the time for considering applications or appeals is to be extended. We are grateful for that information. Why a clause to that effect was not included in the present pension bill, I do not know. It may be added yet; but notwithstanding the fact that we are just about at the end of the present session of parliament, many more clauses might be added. We can hold this House in session; if the minister is prepared with his amendments, let us consider them now. To my mind it is a disgrace to allow parliament to prorogue without passing something in the nature of a remedial pension bill that will take care of a class of cases just such as those which have been pointed out so well in this House this afternoon and evening, and I am sure that the manner in which they have been pointed out must have impressed the ^ minister with the seriousness of the situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I have
listened with the greatest interest to the discussion which has taken place in this chamber this afternoon and evening. Perhaps the House will permit me to say that I have had a little experience in connection with pension matters and ex-service men's problems. At the outset let me say that at least three-quarters and perhaps ninety-five per cent of the cases which I have heard cited here this

Pension Act-Mr. Ralston
afternoon and to-night could be dealt with and, if they are legitimate, should be dealt with, as matters not of legislation but of administration.
I have gone through the amendments Which have been suggested at the present session by representatives of that splendid organization, the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League, and in the forty amendments which have been suggested I do not think there is a single one which will cover one of the cases that have been cited here to-day. Primarily it is not more legislation that we need in connection with pension matters. There are only two things required: first, a tribunal which, as has been suggested, will view in a sympathetic way the legislation which it administers and the cases which come before it, and second, reasonable evidence to connect the disability, whatever it may be, with the service period.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) has suggested that the Pension Act is much too circumscribed. I do not know very much about pension acts of other nations, but I may remind the House that the only thing which is required in order to entitle a man to a pension is that the disability from which he is suffering has 'been not caused by service, but incurred during service. In other words if it had its inception during service, if a man were on leave in London, England, or Canada and contracted some disease, automatically under our Pension Act he is entitled to pension.
For any disease?

The hon. member for
Kingston possibly has regard to immoral cases. My hon. friend knows that the tribunal has discretion to allow pensions in such cases. The real things required are a sympathetic tribunal and the securing of reasonable evidence. I happen to belong to the legal profession. There are in this House some members belonging to the medical profession. When a member of the medical profession says that by no possibility could the disability in a certain case have been incurred during service, it is difficult under the act for a board of pension commissioners, sympathetic as they may be, or for this House or for any other tribunal, to make a different finding, unless you have some sort of act which states that regardless of when the diesase or disability was incurred, the man is entitled to pension just the same.

May I ask a question
just on that point? because the minister is an authority on this subject and we are all keenly interested in it. Has he not found that the
pension board always take the stand that the question is not one of sympathy; that they are interpreting strictly the law as written in the statute? They say:	We are not a
sympathetic body; we want to find out what the law is, and we are applying the law. Let parliament attend to the sympathetic side of the question.

As I have said, that is the act which they administer, and I am not standing here in any way defending the Board of Pension Commissioners or the Federal Appeal Board. I am stating what are the proper requisites to the administration of the Pension Act, and that the important thing is not so much legislation as administration. I have also pointed out that the amendments which have been suggested are not amendments which cover the cases that have been cited here to-day.
We must have machinery to carry out the Pension Act. Somebody must decide these questions. It is out of the question for this high court of parliament, even possessing the ample jurisdiction which it does, to attempt to consider and to pass upon all these cases. That would not be fair to the country or to the ex-service men. Neither is it possible for a committee of this House to do this. Some machinery must be set up whereby there can be a reasonable and proper adjudication oi these claims. The Board of Pension Commissioners was established in 1917, before this government took office, and when a commission, which has been referred to to-day, came to consider the matter, it was found that three men sitting in the city of Ottawa could determine the rights of people who had been injured during the war, their widows or other dependents, and could commit the country to millions of dollars of expenditure, and that their decision was final. It was felt that that was neither right nor fair to the country or to the ex-service men.
The suggestion has been made that this government has done nothing. I am not going to make a political speech, but I feel that statement should not be broadcast without the history of the legislation being understood. What was done? An act was passed in 1923 providing for a federal appeal board. I want to tell my hon. friends who have spoken that there is no appeal in connection with the widow in the case cited by the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) this afternoon. Under the legislation which passed this House in 1923-and I have the bill under my hand-there was an appeal in those cases
Pension Act-Mr. Ralston

There was an appeal in every case as recommended by the commission. It was not in this House that that appeal was refused, but when the bill came back to this House it was found that the only case in which an appeal was allowed was when it had been decided that the disability had not been incurred during service.
Mr. CLARK I would like my hon. friend
to make it quite clear that there is no appeal in the case I cited this afternoon. It is purely discretionary.

Certainly, that is what I am saying, and I am pointing out that that was not the fault of this House of Commons As the legislation passed this House, an appeal was given in every case, as to the amount of pension, as to whether a widowed father or mother was in dependent circumstances, meaning such circumstances that they had not sufficient to provide themselves with . a living, and also in the many cases which arise in connection with collateral questions. But all these appeals were cut out in the other House, and the only appeal allowed was when the decision was given on the ground that the disease or disability was not incurred during service. That was one thing that was done.
What else was done? It was found that complaint was made also that a man had a pretty stiff road to travel in connection with proving his claim for pension. He did not understand very much about pension law. All he knew was that he was sick, and he felt the war was the cause, and so the suggestion was made, and was put in the statutes of this country, that in every district there should be a man, nominated by the ex-service men's organizations and paid by the government of this country, whose job it would be to present the case of any man who went to him in connection with appeals under this act. I think that was a step in the right direction. It improved the machinery for helping the ex-service man to get his claim properly adjudicated upon.
But still there is always the question of evidence. I think I can say that there come to my desk as many cases with regard to pensions as to the desk of any member of this House except the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King, Kootenay). The first thing I do is not to blame the pension board or the appeal board, but to get the record of the case and look at it myself to try and find where the hole is, to see what evidence is wanting and whether there is any possibility of getting it. Then I
	*
immediately write the man or his doctor to see if evidence cannot be given to show that during some particular period after his discharge and before his disability seems to have been recognized, the man was ailing, in order to show that the disability he now has can be related more or less continuously back to the time of his service. That is always the difficulty, and it is growing as the years go on. We are now ten years from the war, and there is no doubt that every year- and I do not blame the members of the medical profession-it is harder every year for them to certify that the particular disease or disability which now exists was incurred away back there. My theory is-and this is where the matter of administration comes in mostly-that if, taking all the evidence, it is shown to have been reasonably possible that the disability which is now being suffered could have been incurred during service, that constitutes a reasonable doubt in favour of the man and the pension should be awarded. Let me put it in other words, and I know my words are not binding on any judicial tribunal:	Suppose I were on the pension
board and with respect to a given case, having read the files and heard the evidence both ways, had said: "No pension." Then if when I went home at night and put on my slippers, as we all do these days having so much time on our hands, and sat before the fire and thought over -that case and was seriously troubled as to whether after all that fellow was not entitled to a pension; if I had made a mistake, if I had a reasonable doubt that I had not done the right thing, that man it seems to me is entitled to a pension. I say you cannot put that in a statute-never; it is a matter for the tribunal which is administering the act. So I say that when we speak of the pressing need for legislation I am not so sure that any amendments will be found to be a cure for the cases which have been cited. But the commission said: "The board may err; they are only human, and the man ought to have a second chance," and so a federal appeal board was set up. The idea of that appeal board was this: We felt that the men sitting at Ottawa were too far away from the individuals concerned, that they did not get the personal touch. Many men, and perhaps some doctors, have not the ability to give a word picture of a case as* it would be presented to the pension board if they saw the man face to face. There are some things in connection with pension evidence which depend almost wholly on the word of the man; he may be unable to give any corrobora-

Pension Act-Mr. Ralston
tion; he may give a history of having been blown up by a shell when nobody was around at all. The board has then to put the test that is generally put by any jury:	Does he
look like a man who is telling the truth? Look him over and see how he is giving his evidence. What do his neighbours say about his reputation for telling the truth? Do not lay down a rule that there must be corroboration in every case, but decide it on the ordinary principles on which a jury decide a case. If you approach it in that spirit a great many of the difficulties may be solved. And so we said:	We will provide appeal
boards, and the form of appeal boards which passed this House was not the appeal board in the form in which it now appears in the statute. The appeal board this House approved was a series of district review boards; that is, the Dominion was divided into districts, and it was provided that these review boards would travel up and down and see the men face to face; the district review board would make its decision, and the case could then igo to the federal board if the Board of Pension Commissioners or the applicant felt that the decision was wrong, the Federal Appeal Board could review it. A provision was inserted in the statute to the effect that the Federal Appeal Board could not reverse a favourable decision of the district review board unless they actually saw the man, unless he waived that privilege. But a.s I say, the legislation was not adopted in that form. Instead, a federal appeal board was set up, and that federal appeal board, which is the subject of the bill now before the House, has been travelling up and down this country and has given considerable relief in a large number of cases which were thought at least by the citizens at large to be meritorious, decisions being made which are favourable to the pensioner. That is an advance. That is an attempt to provide machinery which may take care of these things. If we sit here till doomsday we cannot decide these individual cases; we must entrust them to some machinery. My view of the subject, therefore, is that our efforts should be directed to making the machinery as complete and as smooth-working and as expeditious as possible.

I would ask the minister if the present pension legislation will permit through administrative means without statutory amendment, of the reopening of a man's case in the event of the discovery of new evidence?

No. My hon. friend will find in the bill of 1923, to which I have referred, that the legislation which passed this House on the recommendation of the commission provided that when new evidence was discovered sufficiently convincing in the opinion of the district review board a fresh appeal might be made, but that also did nol become law. Perhaps my hon. friend was not in the House when the announcement was made that the minister has under his hand now, in connection with amendments to the procedure, an amendment which permits the very thing to which my hon. friend refers, and I understand that the minister will propose that amendment as soon as we get into committee. As I have said, in my humble opinion, that our efforts should be primarily devoted to making as efficient as possible the machinery for hearing these cases. While we may bring individual cases before the House by way of illustration, we cannot get very much further with them here.
I want to remind hon. gentlemen opposite that in past years a good deal of pension legislation has been enacted and many amendments have been made to the act. The amendments that are now being proposed, and others that may be put forward in the future, will not, I anticipate, affect the principle on which pensions are being awarded-the principle that the disability must be incurred during service in order to entitle a man to a pension. I will deal in a moment with cases vi'here disability is not incurred during service and the soldier is sick and needs assistance.

Before the minister
leaves that point, does he not know that right in the country to-day there are thousands of cases that without a shadow of doubt are attributable to war service, but the disease cannot be attached to that service sufficiently to secure a pension?

My hon. friend I hope, will not think I am coming back at him, but he belongs to the profession to which I refer, and I can only say that if there is not a shadow of doubt in those cases, and if the doctors will say so, that is all that is necessary to entitle the men to pensions.
I beg to differ with the hon. minister. That is not the practice.

I do not mean my hon. friend or any individual doctor. The hypothetical case he put was that in which there
Pension Act-Mr. Ralston

was not a shadow of doubt that the disability was incurred during service. Then the pension board's medical advisers or any doctor who has the honour of his profession at heart will so certify.

I do not like to interrupt the minister but what I have in mind is this. There are to-day right in this country hundreds of cases of nervous breakdown, insanity, borderline cases, that every medical man who has had any experience at all is convinced are primarily due to war service; but you cannot get sufficient evidence to attach those cases to war service in order to entitle the men to pensions.

I am only saying that the evidence lies in the hands of the medical man. He has to decide, not the lawyers. If the medical man on his professional responsibility says that the disease, whatever it may be, is connected with war service, and traces it back there, I do not see why a pension is not granted. But my hon. friend gives me an opportunity that I was going to take later of dealing with the class of cases in which, let us say, there is a reasonable doubt, they cannot be proved beyond a shadow of doubt to be due to war service. I refer to the exsoldier who has a breakdown. I am not saying what the policy of the government may be, but I anticipate that in this country there will be established soldier homes to take care of that sort of case. It is the only way you can deal with it. You cannot bring it under any pension legislation unless you can produce the certificate of the medical men or the evidence to which I referred.

The medical men do
not give the pensions; the pension board decide.

My hon. friend knows
that three out of the four members of the pension board' are medical men.
But they are not always guided by medical certificates.

I would not make a
remark of that kind-
I make it.

-about medical men. I know the chief medical adviser of the board very well, and I think he would be guided by the certificates of medical men. I think my hon. friend will agree with me that if he were sitting on a -case as judge he would insist on some reasonable connection of the disability with war service. He would not be satisfied simply by a letter stating, "I certify fMr. Ralston.]
John Jones' disability to-day is due to war service," without the medical man showing that at the -time of discharge he had been ailing or had what was -a continuous condition. My friend says "attributable to service". May I make this clear? I think hon. gentlemen understand it. -I would say, -let' us get -this "attributable 'to service" out of our minds. There is no necessity under the Pension Act to-day to prove that the disease is attributable to service. Service may not have had anything to d-o with it, but if the trouble began during service -that is enough under the Pension Act.
I think in practice they -put it the -other way. I know many such cases.

I am sure of it. That
is -my experience.

I can only speak out of
my own experience, -and I assure -my friend and other hon. members that I have had many, many cases in which I could not show in any -possible way or make any suggestion that the disability was due to service; it was sufficient so long as I proved that the trouble began before discharge.

That was attributable to
service.
No.

You must have
received preferential treatment.

Now, in regard to legislation. It seems to me that 1923 was the beginning of pretty constructive pension legislation. In that year the appeal board was established and the soldier advisers appointed. It was suggested this afternoon that we had not had very much pension legislation. I want to remind the House that the case which was regarded by us as entitled to sympathetic treatment, namely, the widow who had received commutation of pension on remarriage, but had lost her second husband, was provided with a pension under the bill passed in 1924, and under the same measure payments to parents were readjusted on a more liberal basis. And this somewhat unusual provision was made. A man receiving 25 per cent for some disability might die, and his death might be due to something totally outside that disability. The provision I refer to is to the effect that payment is to be made to the widow pending investigation of that case to ascertain whether the death was the result of the service disability or not, because if so the widow would be entitled to a pension for life. In the same year a retro-

Pension Act-Mr. Ralston
active pension was provided when a reversal of the decision of the board had been made. Last, but not least, the meritorious clause, so-called, was passed. It was regarded by ex-service men generally as being a very important step. That clause was supposed to make the act more elastic, to use the words of the hon. leader of the opposition, to make it possible to consider cases which would not otherwise be entertained under the act. I understand that a small number of cases have been considered. As hon. gentlemen know, the meritorious clause has to be administered by a joint board consisting of the pension commissioners and the appeal board. I think in connection with that some consideration might be given to a matter of procedure which I have in mind in order to make it more effective.

Has the minister the
figures of that relief?
I understand there have been thirteen cases.
No, eleven.

My hon. friend from Vancouver thought that 1925 was a blank year in regard to pension legislation. He is wrong. During that year a good deal of pension legislation was enacted. For instance, there was an extension of the 80 per cent clause. It was provided that when a man has 80 per cent disability it does not make any difference what causes his death; whether he be killed by a street car or in any other accidental way, his dependents are entitled to a pension providing the death takes place ten years after discharge. Previously the period had been five years. Tuberculosis cases, which everyone has at heart, were dealt with. There are no cases which are more sympathetically viewed by the country than those of the tubercular men, and I think the Tubercular Veterans Association will agree that a long step forward was taken when it was provided that any man with tuberculosis, moderately advanced and clinically active, when discharged from the sanatarium, even though the tuberculosis might be arrested, should be entitled to 100 per cent pension to be continued for two years. That, I say, was a long step in advance. In the case of tubercular men who saw no service in a theatre of war the pension is 90 per cent. At the same session at which this provision was made another amendment was passed providing for the reopening of final payments. Provision was made for wear and tear allowance for clothing of amputation cases, namely an allowance cf $54 for these men. Under that provision a good deal of money was paid out and was
warmly welcomed by the returned soldiers. Pensions in connection with misconduct cases, particularly in relation to widows, received sympathetic consideration. Altogether, therefore, considerable progress was made in the session of 1925.
Hon. gentlemen will, I think, realize that some attempt has been made by the government and by this parliament to effect improvements in our pensions legislation. The proposals made at the present time, some of which are included in the memorandum submitted by the British Empire Service League, are largely of two classes: they extend the class of those to whom pensions are to be granted or they increase in some respect the amount of pensions to be paid. They do not change the principle upon which, generally speaking, pensions are given. I do not want to delay the House, but perhaps I may be permitted to refer very briefly to one or two matters as to which proposals have been made. For instance, a man may be receiving a pension on account of what is described as aggravation of disability due to service. Gases of aggravation apply generally only to such men as have not served in any theatre of war, except in one or two instances which I need not refer to. That is to say, any man who has served in a theatre of war is entitled to pension for the total degree of disability which he suffered at the time of discharge, notwithstanding the fact that some part of that disability may have existed before he enlisted. The theory is that if he was fit enough to be taken overseas for service he should be regarded as having been fit in every way, so that the pension should be granted for the full amount of disability from which he suffered on discharge. The provision contained in the proposals of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League is this, that where a man dies who has been pensioned for aggravation alone-where he has not served in any theatre of war-if it can be established that the aggravation of his disability in any way contributed to his death his widow is to be entitled to full pension.
It is also proposed that there should be no suspension of a man's pension without notice to the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. I do not think there is any need for legislation in that respect, because the department will be only too glad, I feel sure, to notify some service bureau in order that the necessary steps might be taken to present the man's case afresh before suspension of pension finally takes place.
Another matter is the consideration of the pension as part of the ex-soldier's estate. The
Pension Act-Mr. Ralston

proposal was made that any portion of a pension unpaid was to form part of the pensioner's estate if he made a will. The suggestion of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League is that, even where there is no will, such unpaid portion of pension should be regarded as part of the estate to be administered by the Board of Pension Commissioners. A further subject of interest relates to children who are suffering from physical infirmity and who receive an allowance. According to the act the only children who may receive any allowance by reason of physical infirmity are those whose infirmity was incurred before the age of twenty-one. The proposal is, as I understand it, that if the son of a soldier killed overseas becomes infirm and is incapacitated from earning a living, even though he may be over twenty-one, he shall be entitled to a pension on account of his father's 'death. Still another proposal is to make the pension more retroactive; it is thought that the payments should be extended further back.
A vexed question which has been discussed in the House on two or three occasions is the position of the widow of the soldier who dies after discharge from the service, and who was married "after the appearance" of disability, to quote the words of the act. A great deal of difficulty arises in connection with the consideration of these words "after the appearance of disability." On two or three occasions an amendment has been passed here, but it has never become law.
I might mention now what is perhaps a peculiar case. As hon. members may probably know, a woman who has been cohabiting with a man as his common law wife is entitled to a pension; but strangely enough, under the act, if the union was subsequently made legal there may be a danger, in the event of her husband's death, of the pension being disallowed. To remove that anomaly a proposal has been submitted.
All these casses I have cited, it will be realized, are but samples, so to speak; they do not touch the cases brought forward in this chamber to-day. Upon some of them the House has expressed its opinion before, while many of them are new. Now, the question to be considered by the government or by anyone responsible for the administration of affairs is, what are meritorious cases and what are not? For example, my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) to-day suggested that this country should assume the responsbility for the burial and medical attendance expenses of the wives and dependents of ex-soldiers. That is a pretty large respon-

sibility. To me it is altogether new. The question in this instance is: would it be better to make such a provision as the hon. member suggests, and leave other cases unprovided for; or, on the other hand, endeavour to make a wider distribution of the benefits to be conferred? These are questions to be carefully considered. The minister has altogether about 200 suggestions looking to the improvement of our pensions legislation and the administration of the act, and I feel, speaking frankly as an ex-service man, that I may safely say that the government is trying its utmost to do justice by the returned soldiers. I do not think I need to express my sympathy with the returned soldiers or tell the House that I am endeavouring in every way I can to see to it that the honourable obligations of the country to the ex-service men are carried out. It is in the interests of the returned men and of the country as well that just and proper consideration should be given to all these proposals regarding the consolidation of the Pension Act, so that next year they may be submitted to a special committee of the House and thoroughly investigated with the result as suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie), of a revised Pension act being enacted if need be. I think, however, it will be found that the Pension Act as we have it is drafted along the proper lines. ' It may be encumbered with amendments and possibly can be simplified, but it seems to me that we should study these proposals and in the light of mature consideration see just what new principles should be embodied in the act.

Is there any remedy or
relief possible through the administration of the present act, or will there be any relief under the proposed amendments, to such a typical case as the one I am about to cite?
I have on my desk several letters, but I may refer to this one in particular because, as I say, the case is typical. I want to read three or four lines from this letter. This is from a returned soldier who has a 25 per cent disability. He says:
It's up to the government to help me out. . . if I can't get government help, I must grin and bear it.
He then refers to the cost of their relief to some one, the municipality or the government, in any case, and goes on to say:
I alone cost the government $100 every winter in relief. That's why I'm fighting for a job. I don't want it

That- is, the relief.
I want work.

Pension Act-Mr. MacLaren
Further Sown in the same letter he says:
I can in summer keep my head up, but in winter it drops. What a glorification in fighting for one's country.
Perhaps we should not blame him for being bitter.
I lost my money in the Home bank, still have $320 to come. . . Robbed of what I had, discharged a 25 per cent disability man. . . .
I think the hon. gentleman might better wait until the bill is in committee before putting such a long question.
I was almost'finished. This man being in receipt of a very small pension, is there any provision under the present act or the proposed legislation for the relief of such cases?

The only relief would
be by way of administration in connection with the provision of employment; that is all I can see in the case. As my hon. friend knows, a superpreference has been given to wounded ex-service men and a preference to ex-service men not wounded, under the Civil Service Act'. I might also say that in connection with the employment, and as his correspondent suggests in connection with relief, a man who has a pension and who is partly disabled is entitled to consideration. These are cases we all come in contact with; they are not unusual at all. They are the cases which, if the country had plenty of work, would occupy jobs running elevators and doing things of that kind. In that way these men could be absorbed, but that is not the case in Canada at present. We always have the difficulty of men who, having the amonut of their disability theoretically at least made up by the contribution of the country, still find themselves because of their handicap not in a good position to compete in the labour market.
I do not want to detain the House any longer; I only wish to repeat that I do feel this to be in the interest of ex-service men, whom I know to be very reasonable. I have met them from the Atlantic to the Pacific in the closest possible way, and I have found that when you meet them face to face and deal with their cases straightforwardly you can get the most frank expression from them, and can give them the same kind of consideration. They were and are as reasonable as anyone could expect, and the difficulty about this thing is the mystery sometimes thrown around it, as I have said, by reason of the fact that they are so far away from the tribunal which decides their cases. Naturally this is a matter in which I have an intense personal interest and it is hardly necessary
for me to say as a member of this government that I know my colleagues are in hearty sympathy with the object we all have in view, and that every endeavour will be made to put this matter in the best possible shape for further action. That wall apply to these proposals and others which have been made by different people; they will be given the most careful and thorough study, and the close attention which the importance of the subjects demands.

The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has made a very clear statement, and I am disposed to agree with a great deal of what he has said. There are two factors in the matter of pensions, the provisions of the act on the one hand and its interpretation and administration on the other, and I believe much misapprehension has arisen through the failure fully to appreciate the importance of both these elements. The Pension Act requires amendment, which is only natural; there is no finality to an act of this character. Pension matters are of great difficulty, and contain many abstruse points; an act of this kind naturally lacks the precision of others, because of the fact that it has to do with human disability. Therefore we must expect amendments from time to time, but however near we approach perfection the act will materially fail unless its interpretation and administration are as efficient as we can hope for.
It is a matter of common experience that a man will make an application time and time again, but his pension will be refused; finally, after a very considerable time, and after much perseverance, he is allowed a pension. Why is that? In the meantime there has been no change in the act or in the requirements, and there may be little or no new evidence presented. I think that is a point which requires the attention of the minister; he should look carefully into the administration of the act, because it will not succeed until it receives the support and proper interpretation of the pension commissioners. I have many times seen the results of the excellent work done by the Canadian Legion; they have assisted men in obtaining their pensions after long periods and after much laborious effort, but I would ask the minister why that should be necessary. I think the attitude of the pension board should be to assist men to put a claim through, rather than to make them fight for it, to decline their applications on a number of occasions and finally grant them on practically the same evidence. Again I

suggest to the minister that he might well study the administration of this act and see if great improvement cannot be effected there. I cannot understand why men should go on being refused for many months, and finally receive their pensions.
