I think it the only correct view, because so far as this House can do so it has paid due attention to the subject of pensions and has made proper provision for the returned men.
We have had this act gone over both by special committees of the House and by a royal commission. We have had prolonged debates in this House and we have not succeeded in satisfying the many claims presented. No doubt the act has been imperfect. We should have a more perfect act, but unless there is a more reasonable attitude on the part of those who have to deal with pensions we can hardly make the progress that we otherwise would.
Was the operation for a war disability?

Yes. When an
operation is performed for something, such as appendicitis, that is not a war disability, I do not think the department should at this time assume responsibility for it. There is no reason for retaining that section. The particular case to which I refer is where a man was being hospitalized for varicose veins and I believe by mistake they operated on his feet. As a result 'the man has not walked since. It is quite true that they say they found out later that the man had a venereal disease. The board had all the evidence before them at the time and they were the only ones who knew he had it, but in spite of that they operated on him. I believe that section should be struck out of the act and that in such a case the man should be given a fair show.
The Minister of National Defence stated that at the time the appeal board was created it was not an appeal board1 that was first suggested. We know that, but at the same time we know that the appeal board to-day, which has done some good work, is being hindered in its activities by one or two things. The Federal Appeal Board cannot change the diagnosis as set down by the Board of Pension Commissioners. In one 'Case we forced them to withdraw that diagnosis. It is a serious mistake that the appeal board has not the power to change the diagnosis, because uipon that diagnosis will often depend the question whether or not a man is eligible for pension. The Federal Appeal Board cannot act in that case and it cannot change the percentage. These are matters of legislation which can be remedied.
Mention has been made to-night of the tuberculosis condition. The department are aware that they have advisers who have no sympathy as regards the effect of gas upon the ex-service man. Dozens and dozens of these cases have come under my observation, and in bringing these cases to the attention of parliament I want to be a little personal. After the conclusion of the war I was offered a position on the 'pension board. I refused because I believe that after my four yeare' service and experience in charge of medical work at the front I could be of more use to the returned man off the board than on it.

I have done my best to show this House that the cases which come up for consideration will be with us until the last days of the last man who served in the war. There seems to be an idea that these cases should be wiped out. The war was a most peculiar one. The weapons employed in it had effects upon the human system that the medical profession had not had to deal with before, and the result is that there are going to arise in men conditions that would not be considered in former wars but which must foe considered in connection with this war. For years I have pointed out that there must be a sympathetic attitude, a new relation of the medical man to the exservice man, and that only those Who have had service at the front can be in a sympathetic relation towards the returned soldier because they have the knowledge and experience in regard to these cases.
There is no question that gas has left effects upon the men. Those who were at the second battle of Ypres will remember that when men who came back affected by gas attempted to return to the front, they dropped dead on the way owing to the condition of their hearts and lungs. I have found all over this country men suffering from the effects of gas. If you have a medical adviser who has never seen the effects of gas and who is constantly non-sympathetic in regard to it, the ex-service man is going to suffer. The board have advisers of that character and on that account the men cannot get sympathetic treatment. I feel that my experience and relations with the ex-service men at the front have put me into a better position than that of others who have not the same experience to deal with some of these cases. I believe, as the Minister of National Defence has said, that the whole secret of this act lies in administration and sympathy. The sections of the act and the regulations must, of course, be followed, but unless you have that sympathy you will not make much headway.
The minister and several other members this evening have referred to the sections that have been strack out of the act or changed in the other chamber. Why can we not reinsert these and send them up to the other House every year until we get satisfaction along these lines? The Minister of National Defence referred to the fact that it was easy to connect disability with service. He took the stand today-and I think if that were accepted it would help a great deal-that if the disability occurred during service the man was entitled to a pension. I would refer him to the case already mentioned where a hemorrhage occurred on service, and yet the man was not granted

Mr. Speaker, I desire to take just a few moments, not because I do not think this subject is worthy of a longer time, but because everything has been well said already.
I would like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) for the very clear way in which he has presented this question, on which he is an expert. I must confess to being a little bit sorry that perhaps from both sides of the House things have been said which seem to have a little partisan ring to them. I have no sympathy with any partisanship in this House, no matter on which side it is, on a question of this kind. This is too vital a matter for partisanship.
I want to say another thing. When it comes to a question of the soldier or the treasury, my sympathy is entirely with the soldier. I believe that the Minister of National Defence has given us the real reason for the difficulty in this whole matter. I believe that if we had a little more sympathetic consideration by the board, a great many of these difficulties would be removed. I had occasion a few days ago to visit the board, and I made this statement, that I did not believe there was one member in the House on either side who wanted the board to interpret this act in any other than a broad and generous spirit, and not in a technical way at all. I want to state in that connection something which may reflect on the pension board or on the board of appeal, or on both; I am not concerned which.
There was a man in my riding who had a difficulty prior to enlistment. That difficulty was the occasion of an operation after enlistment during the time he was on service. Now he applies for a pension. I may say that his condition was hammer toes, one on either
foot. His toes, I suppose, are all right, but on the bottom of each foot- he has very large callouses, so large and bad that he gets around with very great difficulty. The pension board refused him a pension. He then went to the board of appeal, and they decided his case favourably. The case then went back to the pension board for action, and they took the position that because there was no medical category to which the board of appeal could refer that case, they could not act. It seemed to me the difference was the difference between Tweedledum and Tweedledee. I do not believe the man knows really what is the cause of his trouble. All he knows is that he has trouble with his feet, that it is very difficult for him to walk, and while these two boards are arguing where the authority really lies, this man is suffering. I said to them this: In a case of that character you should, in my humble judgment, give the benefit of the doubt to the returned man and see that he gets relief. If we interpret the act in that way, we would not have as much difficulty as we have.
I want to be fair to the board. I have taken many cases before them, and I have received a great deal of sympathetic consideration. We must recognize this fact, that there are many applications for pension, there are two sides to every question, and when a man is turned down he naturally feels aggrieved.
This is not the place to cite cases, but there is one other I might mention. It is that of a farmer-I am not talking for political friends-a well, strong, husky man, a farmer before he went overseas. During his service some rash broke out on his body. I believe they call it eczema, and although I am a medical man I am not quite sure yet just what eczema is. This rash breaks out from time to time. Unfortunately the man does on occasion take a little alcoholic beverage, and he is worse after that. Apparently the pension board is going to insist that this man become a prohibitionist to see if the disease will not clear up under that cure. I do not believe that we should go to the extent of requiring a man to become a prohibitionist, no matter how good that might be. This man is suffering very much; he is a charge upon his friends, yet in spite of all he can do and all his friends can do, he cannot get a pension.
I want to compliment the Minister of National Defence on the very sane and logical viewpoint that he took. If the board will take every case into their sympathetic consideration and interpret the act in a broad and generous spirit rather than concern them-

Pension Act-Mr. Ryckman
selves with technicalities, many of our difficulties will be removed.
I am glad that the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King, Kootenay) is moving some amendments. In some cases that have come before me the difficulty seems to be the length of time provided in the statute during which the soldier may apply for pension. I understand the minister is going to extend the time for two years. May I say to him that if he chooses to do away with the time limit altogether so that a man suffering from a disability due to war service will get a pension, I would be very happy to support him and go the whole limit. It may have been a good thing, up to the present, to have some time limit but I think the time has now arrived when we can give fair and just consideration to all cases irrespective of time limits.

I shall speak for but a moment, but I wish to refer to certain observations which fell from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I thank the minister for his knowledge of the subject and for the information which he imparted to the House. I think, however, that when he reads in Hansard what he has stated he will find that he has left us with a contradiction, and it is this: He said: I find no fault with the pension board; I find no fault with the Federal Appeal Board; the law is there; they administer it. Later on he said: The difficulty is not one of legislation so much as of administration. Now if the pension board are required to administer the law as they find it, and if there is no fault to be found with their administration, we are driven irresistibly to the conclusion that the real fault is in the legislation.
The minister went on to say, in effect, that you could not legislate sympathy into this act. I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that that is just what can be done. I think that discretion can be left to the pension board. You can have regulations, if you like, not cast-iron regulations which they are bound to follow, but well-defined regulations which they will be at liberty to break through ii they feel the case warrants it.
Living as I do in a populous district where there are many ex-service men, numerous complaints reach me. Every member no doubt is approached by many returned soldiers who have a real grievance, and the human heart goes out to these men, especially when convinced in his own mind that the justice of the case is with them. In several cases I have been firmly of the opinion that pen-

sions should have been granted. Suppose the man did not get it, there would be hearing after hearing of his application, but no relief would be forthcoming. If the applicant persevered, as happened in several cases, the board yielded and a pension was granted. Then the idea would go abroad: Oh, it is easy for one man to get relief upon his application, but the other man must fight his way through the woods until finally he takes this fortress as he took positions against the enemy. That should not be the case. I support my leader in this respect. I do think that the act should be generously amended, and I suggest that the Minister of Solders' Civil Re-establishment and the Minister of National Defence retire, and although the time is short before to-morrow, I am confident the two of them could bring in amendments which would satisfy the ex-service men and the country, and would give us at this session the best workable act possible. I conclude from the statement of the minister that we are to have amendments. That notice came late; but better late than never.
Now, with this notice before us, that in committee we are going to consider amendments to this act, I request the government to make those amendments generous so that they will meet every real case that the Minister of National Defence thinks exists at the present time. I am confident if that is done the returned soldiers will be satisfied and the country will be satisfied. There is a duty resting upon us to be absolutely fair to these men. I believe the one thought that animates every member of this House is to be sure that we do not fail to recognize any claim that can possibly be adjusted.

Does not the hon. gentleman think that the amendments which the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment has announced, and to which I referred, providing for a second appeal in cases of newly discovered evidence, will take care of a great number of cases? Does he not think that that perhaps is the most vital legislation outside of removing the bar to extending the time of application?

Perhaps it is, but so far as the application for a pension is concerned I think there should be no time limit. I think the right to a pension is a continuing right. That right may not be established for ten years when the limit is nine. I do not think the applicant should be shut out by any time limit. In my view every case should be dealt with by the board on its merits as it arises and should not be hampered by any time limit. As a matter of fact I think the government last session and again this session should have appointed a committee of the House to deal with pension legislation affecting returned soldiers and their dependents, and having failed to do so, it being their policy apparently, the government should have prepared the necessary legislation without the assistance of a committee of the House. They are well equipped to prepare that legislation without any assistance from private members, for they have the Board of Pension Commissioners, they have the appeal board, they have the Department of Nationa' Defence, they have the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment with all their experienced and well-qualified staff to advise them, and I am sure that every member of the staff would be willing to devote his best abilities to that work.
Now, in addition to any suggestions that private members might make as to legislation, the government has before it, as has every member of the House, no less than thirty-eight amendments suggested by the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. These amendments have been put forward after careful consideration and discussion by men well qualified to deal with such matters. Following the suggestion made by the hon. member for East Toronto, I would suggest
Pension Act-Mr. Esling

that the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and a small select committee take the matter under consideration even at this late stage of the session and endeavour to bring in additional legislation to alleviate the hardships now being suffered by some of our ex-service men. I do not think any member of this House would begrudge the time necessary to enact such legislation, even though it should necessitate the continuation of this session for a number of days.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer a word more directly in connection with the amendment proposed in Bill No. 234. It is to be regretted that there is not a single amendment offered as a result of the Winnipeg convention and the suggestions placed before the minister. What he offers is merely for the purpose of changing the numerical complexion of the appeal board. It seems to me that at least one of the several amendments suggested by the service bureau of the Canadian Legion might be considered in connection with the amendments to this bill. Take for instance the Soldiers Insurance Act. There is not a member of this House who has not received telegrams and letters urging that the Soldiers Insurance Act be continued. It would not require a new administrative staff inasmuch as that division of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is already functioning. The staff is at present engaged in the payment of claims and the collection of premiums. It would seem from the reports that during the past year the soldiers' insurance division of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment paid 221 claims and collected premiums amounting to about $1,000,000. It has about $4,250,000 on hand, it has 20,000 policies in force and about $59,000,000 worth of insurance. All that is required is an amendment to the bill to continue that insurance machinery in operation.
I want to say a word about this amendment, the purpose of which it is difficult to understand. The minister will correct me if I am wrong in the statement that the act provides that the board shall be composed of not fewer than five and not more than seven members. The minister by his amendment asks for authority to reduce that number; he wants to provide for a board consisting of not fewer than three and not more than seven. One wonders just what this appeal board does. Take the report submitted by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. It contains sixty pages and there is not a full line in the whole document relating 
to the activities of the Federal Appeal Board. Every branch of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is dealt with in detail; all the accounts of the innumerable activities of the department are set forth; but when it comes to the Federal Appeal Board mention is made of it in only three instances. In one case there is mention of $150,000 for the purpose of the board; in another case there is a reference to $31,000 for salaries for the appeal board; and there is another mention of $6,000 also for salaries. But there is not one solitary reference to anything, the appeal board has done or whert. it has held its sittings; no mention is made of its activities. There are two pages in the report giving a table of contents, and you cannot find in that table any reference to the Federal Appeal Board. One wonders therefore, I say, what the board has accomplished. This board is supposed to conduct its activities in every part of the Dominion and in order to facilitate the work the Dominion is divided into eight units. There is one for Quebec, one for the mari-times, one for eastern Ontario, one for central and western Ontario, and there are four for the four western provinces. I should like to have the minister make it clear what his object is in wishing to reduce the membership of the Federal Appeal Board. Certainly it cannot be for the purpose of facilitating the disposal of the applications of men who have not had their pensions granted by the pensions board. We must naturally assume that when an appeal is taken to the Federal Appeal Board the case is a deserving one. Now what is the situation? There are eight units in which this appeal board is supposed to carry on its investigations, and in every one of these units the appeals to-day are precisely one year behind. I can cite one unit in which last year there were 1,400 appeals, of which number fifty were disposed of. If therefore there are no new appeals to be added to the list, it will take just twenty-seven years to dispose of the appeals that are before that one unit.
What unit is that?

Montreal. In view of that fact is there any common sense in the minister presenting such an amendment as this? When the bill comes before the committee I intend to offer an amendment to provide that the Federal Appeal Board shall consist of nine members so that it may function in quorums of three each and in that way carry on its operations throughout the Dominion with some hope of disposing of some of the applications before the poor fellows pass away.

Mr. PETER MoGIBBON (Muskoka-On-tario): I rise to put oa record some statements in answer to the observations of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). There is no finality to this question, nor will there be any, and the sooner parliament and the country realize that fact the sooner we shall get some legislation passed which will be satisfactory to returned soldiers. According to the answer the minister made me, it is easy for anyone to get a pension. All that is necessary is for some doctor to certify to the ex-soldier's disability having been caused by the war, and the pension is granted.

I did not say "some
doctor"; I said the medical adviser to the pensions board.

That restricts it very
much. It leaves it to one or two men who happen to be on the board.

I assume that they are
honest men. If they are not they should be removed and replaced by others in whom the country can have confidence.

I am not referring to the medical men on the pensions board; I am not discussing them. I am referring to the difficulty ex-soldiers experience in getting pensions. ' It has been the experience of every medical man after presenting evidence to the board to have it turned down without due consideration. The minister was right in the statement that the whole thing resolved itself largely into a question of administration and sympathy. Sympathy is the thing which is largely wanting. I know that the members of the board are first-rate men, but like everyone else who has spoken, I think they consider themselves a body which should protect the treasury of Canada. That seems to be the outstanding consideration to them, rather than that of seeing that justice is done the men who have served overseas.
As I said a few moments ago, there is no getting away from the fact that we have arising to-day upon the medical horizon diseases and conditions which were never known before. For example, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) referred to the gas attacks. We have to-day, arising in the lungs, and the minister will bear me out in this, conditions of primary carcinoma which was practically unknown before, and nearly all of such cases which have come under my knowledge have been cases of soldiers who went through gas attacks. The plain assumption is that the irritation of the gas-because irritation is one of the great causes of cancer-has been the primary cause of the later 32649-132
developing carcinoma. We cannot prove it; we would not expect a medical man on any board to say that we could prove it, but it is common sense to make that deduction. Every man is more or less gifted with that quality, and when he sees certain conditions following certain causes, common sense connects them up. For instance, if you see a wreck on the shore you naturally conclude that there has been a storm. We have other diseases of the lungs which we did not know before; we have mental diseases and nervous diseases which we can hardly classify. I think the best diagnosis I ever heard made was given by a witness before the pension committee, when he said the patient was like a battery which was discharged. It is hard to put a name to a condition of that kind; you cannot do it, but at the same time every medical man and every other man will admit that there are a lot of those men who have had something taken out of them through their service which cannot be put back; they are like batteries which cannot be recharged. Then you go on to the border line of diseases of insanity. Look at the wave of crime sweeping over the country, and see how often the criminals are ex-service men. Go a little further, and see how our asylums are being filled up; see how men eight or ten years after the war are breaking down and going insane when there has never before been any evidence of insanity in their family history. These are. new conditions which I claim are attributable to war service; I admit that' you cannot connect them up and you cannot say they are absolutely due to war service, as the minister asks. You cannot prove it because it is something new in the realm of medicine, but the day is coming when it will be recognized as a fact. There is a whole list of new diseases and conditions which are rising on the medical horizon which are no doubt due to war service. These people are not getting pensions; they are disabled; something has been taken out of them which cannot be replaced, and the day is coming when that fact will be recognized. That is the reason I say there is no finality to questions of this kind. These questions are not easy;
I sympathize with the minister and with the Board of Pension Commissioners, because it is a very difficult matter and I believe it will become more difficult to administer this law with justice to the .applicants and justice to the state as the years go by.
Before I leave that point, let me remind the minister about his appeal board. I have no objection to his reducing it and I would have no objection if he wiped it out, as I

Mr. McGIBBON; It is the same thing. They might be convinced that the primary board were wrong in their diagnosis and that the man had something else wrong, but they cannot change the diagnosis. Mr. Speaker, we all listened with a great deal of interest and sympathy to the remarks made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston); I think we all realize that probably no man in this House gave as much consideration, attention and constructive effort to the act as did the minister. He said that he thought the failure was more administrative than legislative; well, hardship has occurred somewhere, and it may be that the administration has broken down. If so, that should be changed.
I fancy my experience does not differ very much from that of other members of this House. More than half the correspondence I receive from my constituents has to do with cases of this kind, and there is a feeling in the country-I am not blaming the government, I am not blaming the minister-that the situation is one that should be dealt with by parliament. Unfortunately it is not being dealt with, or if it is, only to a very limited extent. Now I think that is regrettable, and parliament should not prorogue without some effort being made by constructive legislation to meet a situation which is causing a very great deal of disquiet in the country. That there is disquiet there can be no possible doubt. The fact is brought home to me daily, or at least weekly, by the correspondence I receive; and on occasions when I have returned home I have been approached time and again, in the country and in the towns by men and by their relations seeking to have grievances redressed. I tell the minister, as well as the government and parliament, that a feeling is being aroused which should not exist in this country, and something effective should be done at once to allay that feeling.

Pension Act-Mr. Bennett

In common with most members of the House, I suppose, I have received telegrams from the Canadian Legion suggesting that I remain in my place here long enough to enable the government to deal with those amendments to the Pension Act which in the opinion of the service men are so essential to their wellbeing; and the suggestion I have to make, after listening to the very luminous observations of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is that he and the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King, Kootenay) take a day and frame such amendments as they think may reasonably meet the situation for the year, and put them in as amendments to the present bill. I do not think that is asking too much, and it would do a great deal to calm-I will not use quite as strong a word as agitation-to calm the feelings of those who have considered this matter with much care, namely, the men themselves and their representatives at Winnipeg.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence upon the very interesting statement he made upon the subject. It was characterized by moderation and clarity, and I am sure was a very important contribution to the literature upon the subject so far as this House is concerned. My experience-and I am bound to say it has been very considerable, because one is constantly being interviewed by those who are affected-leads me to conclude that the commissioners have hardened in their interpretation of the act. That is, in the early days of its administration they placed upon it a more sympathetic and broader interpretation than they now do, and there has been a steady hardening, if I may use that word, with respect to the interpretation of the act itself. That has been brought about by many causes. One has been a desire to save the exchequer from the insistent demands upon it. Another has been the feeling that at times the commissioners have been imposed upon. I know of my own knowledge cases in which, under the earlier interpretation of the act, pensions have been awarded that should not have been awarded. The Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment has seen the list that was prepared at one time in this respect, and it has caused a very great deal of feeling in the community. You see A receiving a pension and B, who feels that his claim is quite as strong, not receiving one because the claim for it was made years after the pension had been awarded to A, and there is a consequent feeling throughout the community that an unfairness has been done to B.
32649- 132i
Now, as I see it you have two classes: first, the soldier himself, and secondly the dependents. Among the dependents 'I include the wife, the widow, the mother and the children. With respect to the soldier himself there is one branch of the matter that I have not heard mentioned to-night, in connection with which there has been a very serious hardship upon the applicants. For instance, a soldier applies for a pension. Almost from superficial observation his condition is apparent to the layman. The doctor certifies as to his medical condition. He is told that he cannot receive a pension because his condition is attributable to his pre-war state of health. I have many of these cases. They say:	We cannot give1 you a pension because
upon analysis of your record of health we find that the disability of which you speak could not have been incurred during service but must be attributable to your pre-war condition. I doubt not the Minister of Health remembers some of these oases and every member of this House has heard of them. Now think of the unfairness of that. The Minister of National Defence will tell you as a lawyer that a man in private life who carried on his business in that way would be estopped absolutely from setting that up as a defence. Yet the pension board has set up that defence times without number, and has said that the applicant shall not receive a pension because his condition was not attributable and they use these words-to "war service but to his condition of health prior to his enlistment." Now my contention is that if the man's health was such that he could pass an examination and be certified as a fit and proper person to serve his country overseas it should not lie in the mouth of the department to say that his condition is a pre-war condition. I regret to say there are a great many of these cases and they have given me a good deal of worry. Not long since I discussed this matter with an imperial officer-perhaps he will object to my mentioning his name-who gave me some information with respect to conditions in England. Now as I understand it, in England parliament set up a committee of appeal composed of members of the House of Lords and they heard ten thousand cases, and if his records are correct not less than six thousand cases were favourably considered. The minister will tell you whether or not that is a fair statement of the matter because he has given a great- deal of attention to it. It indicates the frailty of humanity, the weakness of human judgment, the possi-

Pension Act-Mr. Bennett
bilities of error. Surely we can lay down this principle-that any man who has been accepted by the nation as being in fit health to serve the state cannot have it urged against him that the condition in which he finds himself after the war is attributable to pre-enlistment days.

I think my hon. friend's case, if he will permit me, must be the case of a man who has not served in an actual theatre of war, because section 11 of the Pension Act says exactly what my hon. friend claims should be the law. I will read it:
(b) No deduction shall be made from the degree of actual disability of any member of the forces who has served in a theatre of actual war on account of any. disability or disabling condition which existed in him at the time at which he became a member of the forces; provided that no pension shall be paid for a disability or disabling condition which at such time was wilfully concealed, was obvious, was not of a nature to cause rejection from service, or was a congenital defect.

I would have thought, as the minister has said, that that clause was broad enough. I quite agree with what the minister says. I am not going to give names and multiply cases because it is quite obvious that we must rest on generalities if possible and leave particular cases to be dealt with as they arise. I would have thought that the law was broad enough if it were not for the cases that have come under my own observation. I have been unable to have them successfully dealt with because it could not be said that the condition of the men was attributable to the cause alleged, but that the condition complained of was attributable to a pre-enlistment cause, and therefore the pension was not payable. That is the position taken, but it would not be open to very much discussion in a court of law. But they go a step further. They draw a sharp distinction between those who served in a theatre of war and those who did not. The minister has stated to-night, and I took down his words, "that the right of claim arises out of service during the war." Those were his words- "service during the war".

Incurred during service, was it not?
M,r. BENNETT: Incurred during service, the word " service " meaning the length of time that had elapsed from the date of enlistment until discharge. Under the statute that is the definition of service. Therefore if the injury complained of occurred during service, whether in the theatre of war or not, the minister and myself would say that undoubtedly the right to pension arose.

I regret to say-and there must be other hon. members who have had the same experience-that numbers of men have been unable to obtain pensions. It was only a few days before I came to Ottawa that a man came into my office and pointed out to me his condition and circumstances. He could not get a pension because they said: The condition of which you complain to-day was a condition present when you enlisted, and your present condition is entirely due to your pre-enlistment condition of health. That is a wrong attitude for this country to take. I would suggest that during Saturday my hon. friend could make the statute clearer so as to make it apparent to anyone who desires to read it that this state will not set up, against the man who has been accepted to serve- whether in a theatre of war or somewhere else, but at least in the service of the country overseas-a condition which is not in accordance with that of the medical officer who examined him for service.
During the last year or two I have seen some case3 of singular hardship. One wonders why it is that a condition was allowed to continue which made it possible for pensions to be awarded in cases where one could not understand why they were awarded, while in other cases pensions were refused where it was difficult to understand why the refusal should be made.
The board are apparently not trying to save money then?

Not in those cases. That is the point I desire to make. The time has come when something should be done to remove these anomalies. Is it not a fact that in England they found it necessary in the House of Lords to set up this tribunal? The minister has given the matter so much attention that I am sure he will remember that. I thought at one time a small committee of this House, sitting in camera in the early days of a session, might reconsider and deal with many of these pensions in the light of the added knowledge that has come by reason of our having more complete records than we had when the pensions were awarded. But that would not meet the case. What must be done is to make this act so clear in its meaning that, however desirous those who administer it may be to place upon it a hard and technical interpretation, they can not and will not be permitted to do so.
What the minister has said about sympathetic administration comes down after all to this. Men who conceive it to be their duty to interpret a statute may well be within their rights in narrowly construing it and

Pension Act-Mr. Bennett
barring out numbers of deserving cases. Other men actuated by different considerations may place upon the same words a wider and more generous and sympathetic interpretation. We know how in statutes of this character various interpretations have arisen. I suggest with some deference to the minister or ministers that the real fact is that the Pension Act to-day is being construed as a criminal statute-and I do not use the word offensively -whereas in the early days it was construed in accordance with the general principle of civil jurisprudence. We say in criminal law that the onus of proof rests upon the crown and that the crown must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. As the Pension Act is now being interpreted by the board, they have placed upon the applicant the onus of proving his case beyond a reasonable doubt just as the crown must do against the accused in a criminal case.
In a civil case the plaintiff must establish his contention by preponderance of testimony, the distinction between criminal and civil matters being "beyond a reasonable doubt" on the part of the crown in the crimnal case and "preponderance of testimony" with respect to civil matters. In the early days I think it is quite clear that the pension law of the country was administered on the principle of preponderance of evidence. There being no evidence against the case set up by the applicant, he got his pension or his dependent got it as the case might be. If I were compelled to do so, I could cite cases in which it seemed to be reasonably clear that pensions should not be awarded. But there was no counter case set up; the preponderance of evidence was that of the applicant, and that was the end of the matter. In later days, however, by the hardening of the board in the interpretation of the act, they have now compelled the applicant to establish his case beyond a reasonable doubt. I have had numerous cases brought to my 'notice-and this is part of the gratuitous service, the only service a man can do for those (yho have served in the war-in which I have found that hardening and that the attitude of the board was to compel the applicant to establish his case beyond a reasonable doubt.
In an action for negligence, as the Minister of National Defence would say, the onus is upon the plaintiff to establish the negligence and then he has to connect the negligence with the injury complained of. But the judge will always instruct the jury that, if there is any evidence from which they may infer a disregard of duty that brought about the injury complained of, the verdict must be for the plaintiff. Should some such principle as that
not govern in these cases? If there is any evidence from which it might be reasonably inferred that the condition complained of is referable to the service as a cause, the pension should be awarded. Would that be an unfair proposition? I regret to say that is not the attitude with which the matter has been recently approached.
This House owes a great debt to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark). I noticed in the earlier remarks this afternoon a tendency to refer to the matter as being somewhat political in its nature, but I know there is no intention on the part of any hon. member to treat it as a political matter. Some might make remarks that might be thus construed, but none of us has a thought of partisanship or party politics in dealing with the matter. When the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard brought this subject to the attention of the House this afternoon I was a little surprised and hurt that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who is usually generously inclined, should have for a moment alleged unworthy motives against the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. That hon. member was not in the least concerned about his private or personal feelings. What he felt was that there had been a hardening of mind, of interpretation by the board, which brought about a condition which he thought should be dealt with by this parliament. Who is here tonight who does not think it was well worthy of being brought to our attention in order that we might focus our minds on the injury done in a deserving case and on the methods necessary to remedy that wrong?

Would the hon. member suggest to the minister or the House what remedy there is against this hardening of heart or of mind? These members of the board are appointed for ten years. What can we do? We cannot dismiss them. Why criticize them if we cannot do anything with them?

The hon. member for
Quebec South has not exhibited the usual resourcefulness of his very fertile mind. He knows far better than I that all we have to do is to add to the Pension Act a single paragraph stating that, in determining whether a pension should or should not be granted, the principle that applies in an ordinary action for negligence might well be applied. Something of that sort is all that is necessary. In other words, the members of the board might be instructed by the statute itself that they were to apply those broad and generous rules of interpretation to which the minister so
Pension Act-Mr. Bennett

properly referred this evening, rather than those hard and fast technical rules that make for what you might call regard for high precedent, but work a very great hardship on the soldier.

The hon. member would
give the board greater discretion than they now have? I would refuse to do that.

I would respectfully
differ from my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power). I do not usually differ from him. But it is not a question of discretion; it is a question of imposing upon the board by statute a rule of interpretation.

Which they may or may
not follow.
Which they must follow or be impeached.

If the hon. gentleman will
move the impeachment of any member of the board, I will gladly support him.

I am bound to say, Mr. Speaker, that I have not yet before me any such evidence as would warrant me in concluding that the judgment which my hon. friend has just expressed represents his very mature consideration of the subject.
I have thought of it for the last five years, ever since Colonel Thompson has been chairman of the board.
I am bound to say that I believe Colonel Thompson to be an exceedingly fair-minded man, and I am sure the hon. member for Vamcouver-Burrard so believes, as well as my hon. friend from Quebec South.
He is fair-minded.

But if in any statute
placed before Colonel Thompson there is a .provision that a rule of interpretation is to be followed, I know that he is a good enough citizen and also a good enough lawyer to follow it, and therefore this parliament can easily deal with that matter.
One word with respect to the appeal board. The minister pointed out, very properly, the various stages through which the legislation has passed. We were a new country to war when we went into the conflict; we were unaccustomed to its effects and its disasters, and we placed on the statute books in the first instance a pension law that represented the best views we could obtain from other countries. We have amended and supplemented that law as a result of our own experience, largely
[Mr. Bennett.
through the painstaking and persevering efforts of the gentleman who now presides over the Department of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) when he was chairman of the commission appointed to do that work. We provided for an appeal board. Another house of parliament concluded that the provisions in the draft act were not such as to commend themselves to their judgment. I am bound to say that I was rather inclined to think they were right, for this reason:	It is important that
there should be uniformity of administration, and if you have four or five boards scattered throughout Canada, each one approaching the problem from a different standpoint and giving out different judgments, depending on the intellectual capacity and general attitude of mind of the members of those boards, you would have chaos; for the man in the east would say: "Look at the generous way in which the board has treated me," while the man on the Pacific slope -might say; "Look at the technical way in which they have treated me." It was to overcome that difficulty that when the bill -came down from the other House it contained a provision for the appointment of a permanent appeal board to travel throughout Canada and hear these cases, thereby ensuring a measure of uniformity of administration. I do regard uniformity of administration as. of the utmost importance in order 'to satisfy the -claims of those who are most concerned. I think the minister will see that there is much warrant for and,much merit in that contention.

That is exactly what was stated in the report, that there was necessity for uniformity. The suggestion of a central board was made in order to see to it that there should be uniformity of decision, so that the pension board itself could in a case in the west, for instance, correct a decision which was not in accord with the principles under which the act was interpreted generally. The advantage of the district boards was that they would see the man at first-hand, decide quickly, and !be able to dispose of seventy-five per cent of the cases without reference to the central board.

The only difficulty being that it set up two forms of machinery, the central board in addition to the pension board, and the district boards in the military districts; in other words, the district board heard the case first, and reported to the board of appeal here, and they made a judgment. Now the essence of a -court of appeal is that it should be of at least equal knowledge we

Pension Act-Mr. Dennett
will say, and of equal intellectual capacity and power as the court from which the appeals are taken. I am sure the minister will agree that it was intended in the first instance that the appeal board should not be of a permanent character-we all realize that the pension board has come to stay for many years-but was in essence a temporary tribunal created for the purpose of bringing about the determination of the granting or refusing of pension upon evidence which they would take on the ground, as distinguished from evidence that might be presented to the pension board sitting in Ottawa. That is the general principle.
That was why the provision was made in the recommendation that this board at Ottawa should not reverse a decision of the district board without actually nearing the man.

Quite so. That, you see, involved again two movements of the board. The district bo^rd take the evidence, and then they report here, and a reversal of the board's judgment would necessitate their also seeing the man.
No, they did not report at all unless the Board of Pension Commissioners appealed the case.
Quite so.
It stood unless appealed.

It involved three sets of machinery-the district board, the Board of Pension Commissioners, and the board of appeal. The other House, for reasons that I have always thought were fairly sound, concluded that if we had a pension board and a board of appeal, which board of appeal was a moving court, something like going out on assizes and actually seeing the men and hearing the cases, that would be far better than the other method. Here is a difficulty and a very practical one. You can see how difficult it is for a pension board, after it feels that it has given mature consideration to a case and arrived at a right conclusion, to change its mind merely because some other tribunal which they think is.not so well equipped in any way has arrived at a different conclusion.
That is what happens in England.

I know, and my hon.
friend from Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGib-bon) has just made observations with respect to what took place in the appeal board as compared with the pension board. Let me put
this case which my hon. friends from Quebec have seen in the press lately. The appeal board decided that A was entitled to a pension. They so reported; the pension board refused to award pension, and that unfortunate soldier has gone to the courts of this country to secure a mandamus to compel the pension board to do what the board of appeal says the soldier is entitled to have done. Now that is all wrong, and it must be.undone by some method. I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was dealing with the case before he went away, and I doubt not that the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) is now giving it his attention because it is a public scandal that a tribunal set up for the purpose of rectifying a grievance done to a returned soldier should, after a report has been made entitling him to a pension, refuse him a pension because the board did not have sufficient confidence in the court of appeal to carry out its awards. Of course the action was improperly taken, and it has given rise to a good deal of discussion. All that is wrong, and I am sure the minister will say so.
My hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario also had in mind a case which he mentioned to me just after he sat down. He endeavoured to secure a pension for a nurse who had been refused a pension by the pension board. The hon. member went to the court of appeal on her behalf, and the appeal board said that the woman was entitled to a pension. Did she get it? She did not. Now I put this to my hon. friend. Will anything but legislation cure that evil? All the broad comprehensive rules of interpretation and the most sympathetic administration will not change the vital fact that to-day the pension board refuses to pay a pension which the appeal board set up by this parliament has said the applicant is entitled to receive. Surely we must undo that this session. Surely we must not wait until next session for it. Surely my hon. friend between now and Monday will devise a short amendment that will cover that, knowing as I do the ability and facility of expression of my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence.
I have spoken much longer than I intended, but I do press on the government, first of all, this consideration:	that in providing for
pensions on a broad and liberal basis they but express the general attitude of mind of all the Canadian people. Secondly, that under our institutions any measures involving expenditure of public money must originate with the government; therefore when we press these matters on them we do so not as a party, but
Pension Act-Mr. Price

rather as individual members of parliament who look to them to give effect to what we conceive to be the will and the wish of the people. Thirdly, that in view of the promises made and the way in which last session ended, it is not too much to suggest that between now and Monday the hon. ministers may be able to prepare such amendments as will relieve the most pressing of the grievances indicated by the soldiers themselves. I say the most pressing. I am not unfair enough to suggest that the two hon. gentlemen could meet all the various conditions in the short time at their disposal; quite the opposite, and I know they have given this matter perhaps much more consideration than any of us. I also know of the pressure of public business and the difficulty of concentrating on many problems to the exclusion of all others that they have to deal with in the public interest. I do not say that many of these recommendations cannot be met by a moderate, well-tempered and sympathetic interpretation of the present statute. I agree with the minister in that, but I do say that one or two, if not three, of the matters to which I have ventured to refer to-night cannot be dealt with in that way.
Not one of them is dealt with in these proposals.

I think the minister will agree that the suggestions are certainly such as in practice we have all come up against. I am only speaking out of the fulness of my heart. I only know what I have seen. It reminds me of the story of an unfortunate claimant for a pension. Not getting it at the first attempt, after a long time he tried again, but with no better success, and he was told that his ill health was attributable to pre-war conditions. He was a man who read his Bible much, and his temper still had not been frayed. So he told me he was like the man who in Scripture had been cured of his blindness, and on being asked about how it happened said, "I only know that whereas I was blind now I see." Said this poor unfortunate soldier, " All I can say is this, that wheTeas before I went to the war I was sound,
I now know I am a broken derelict." I thought it was an excellent answer.
These matters to which I have referred, perhaps at greater length than necessary, are matters that cannot be dealt with by any wide interpretation of existing legislation, and I do venture to suggest-not in any party spirit, for I know hon. gentlemen opposite have just as warm a desire as any other hon. members to help t'he returned soldier-that it is not asking too much to expect that 
between now and Monday, say during Saturday-when of course ministers have nothing to do but attend council where they can write these recommendations-they may be able to prepare the necessary amendments in order to give effect to the most pressing demands of the moment. With respect to this particular measure dealing with the appeal board, if in practice it has been found desirable I think the House will be the first to say the bill should be passed. As to insurance, if it can be extended it does not seem to me that from an actuarial standpoint the country is running any very great risk. The cost of management has not involved us in any very great monetary risks because there has been a fair regard for actuarial considerations in the preparation of the tables. The losses have not been greater than were anticipated, and the accumulated funds are as substantial as might be hoped for under the circumstances. In view of these considerations I join in suggesting to my hon. friends that in the short interval be^veen now and Monday they prepare such legislation as will give effect to the most pressing of these grievances.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King, Kootenay), to two very important telegrams which I have received. I will not detain the House by reading all the telegrams which I have under my hand with regard to the Pension Act. The first telegram is from Moncton and is addressed to myself:
Amendments to Pension Act urgently required this session in order to assist in relieving distress among sick and disabled. Your kind cooperation will be greatly appreciated.
E. L. Morris,
Secretary Riverglade tuberculous branch Canadian Legion.
I wish to point out that these boys were gassed at the front, and I am sure if the hon. minister would visit the sanatarium at Riverglade he would appreciate their sufferings. I would ask his particular consideration of these cases. The second telegram is also from Moncton and reads:
Advice received here . government do not intend to consider legislation re pensions and insurance for returned men this session as proposed to them by headquarters of the Canadian Legion. Please press all possible for government's reconsideration of this decision.
L. T. Tingley, Secretary Treasurer.
In view of what the hon. minister said in reply to the question which I placed on the order paper as to whether legislation would be introduced this session to relieve these men.

Pension Act-Mr. King (Kootenay)
who are not now covered by existing legislation, I would ask him if it is his intention yet to introduce such legislation, or does he desire to have the government stand before the people declaring that it has refused to give consideration to these really deserving cases, especially in view of the fact that millions of dollars are being spent t'o-day throughout Canada for purposes not of such import as those which have been brought to the atten-, tion of the government during this debate? The hon. minister will no doubt recognize that thousands of people throughout' the Dominion are watching to see what the government intends to do. It is up to the government to look after the returned men. They have not been properly looked after in the past. Therefore before this session closes the government should show some consideration for the boys who went to the front and for their relatives and their dependents who are in distressed circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The discussion today has, I think, been advantageous and will serve a useful purpose. It must be evident to those on both sides of the House who have listened to what has been said to-day that certain conclusions can be drawn. In the first place, the principle on which our present pension legislation is based is sound; pensions will be paid on account of disability due to war service. That is the primary principle. From the discussion this afternoon there seems to be a feeling among the members of this House that the pension authorities who administer the act are, if anything, too circumscribed within the scope of the legislation. It is difficult to make that statement and it is one that should not be made without fairly mature consideration. It is true that all of us have been interested in cases such as have been mentioned to-day. Before I became minister, as well as since, I have had brought to my attention cases in which I had personal knowledge and I felt that consideration should be given them. Some of these cases have gone to the pension board and on appeal have been rejected. I do not know whether it would be within my right or the right of any member of this House, because he happened to fail in his presentation of a case, to suggest that the machinery of the pensions board had fallen down or that the act was not being properly administered; for I think it is generally conceded, not only in Canada but universally, that the Canadian pension laws are as liberal as, if not more liberal than those of any of the allied nations except possibly the United States. Three or
four years ago a similar feeling prevailed in this House, that the pensions board was not dealing as it should with certain cases. As a result of that impression the appeal board was established and it has served a useful purpose.
There has been brought forward to-day a question, which I might as well consider now as later on, regarding the activities of the board. The appeal board came into being on October 1, 1924. There were entered 10,154 appeals of which 5,122 were disposed of without hearing, there being no jurisdiction. That left a total of 5,032 bona fide appeals, of which 691 have been allowed. There have been disallowed 2,047 while 352 are pending judgment. That makes a total of 3,090 cases considered, leaving still to be heard 1,942. These are the figures submitted to me by the department. The hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) made the statement that there were 1,400 appeals in Montreal still to be heard. What are the facts? In Montreal 236 cases have been disposed of, while cases awaiting disposal number 4, plus 269 which are not yet ready, that is to say, in which the soldier adviser has not sufficient ground on which to proceed with the appeal. So that throughout the country, from Halifax to Vancouver, appeals have been heard and adjustments made to the number of 3,090, while there are 1,942 cases still to be considered.
Regarding legislation which might be brought down this year as suggested, a week or ten days ago I thought it would be fair to the soldier organizations as well as to the House to indicate the line of action the government would be able to take with reference to the matters that had been submitted by the Canadian Legion and other soldier organizations throughout Canada. It is true that representations were made by various bodies and comprehensive memoranda prepared and submitted; it is also true that we had the honour of meeting various officers of these associations in consultation. At that meeting I requested the presence of the chairman of the pension board, the deputy minister of the department, the assistant deputy minister, the medical director and other officers so that they might hear what the returned men had to say. We found, as we considered the various amendments, that many of them were intended to relieve individual cases or small groups; and it was pointed out by the officers who are familiar with the law that many of these cases could be dealt with by administrative means without the necessity for legislative action.

Pension Act-Mr. King (Kootenay)
With regard to tubercular veterans, whom we have heard discussed, I am sure we are all sympathetic in our attitude to these par. ticular returned men. They not only made representations, as was set out in the memorandum to which reference has been made, but they also suggested to me as minister that if it were not possible for legislation to be introduced at this session I should undertake during the recess to convene a meeting of tubercular specialists to give the veterans an opportunity of stating their case to these experts. Since that interview I have instructed the officials of the department to arrange for a convention of that nature and it will be possible for the tubercular veterans, through their representatives, to appear before the specialists this season and make a full statement of their case. Tuberculosis is one of the diseases which after the war filled our sanataria, but to-day we find these cases dwindling in number. There are some new cases developing, and the difficulty in connection with these, eight or ten years after the war, is to establish their connection with military service.
As I stated a few moments ago, it has generally been considered that our pension legislation is generous. We know at any rate that there has not been that hardening which the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has referred to, because in the last five years our pension bill has grown from $30,000,000 to $37,000,000, showing that the bill is being extended from year to year. Now the question is whether we should hastily consider amendments to meet certain representations which have been made at this session, or whether we should deliberately sit down and in close conference develop amendments which could be incorporated into our Pension Act next session, when a proper consolidation of that act may be made.
1 propose to move two amendments which are basic and primary in their character, which are of great importance to the returned soldiers and which I think will be very acceptable to them. The first amendment extends the period in which an application for pension may be filed from seven to nine years, the seven year period expiring this year. This will give two years more in which to file these applications, and from the representations which have been made to us I am satisfied that this is one of the things the men most desire. On account of the seven year period expiring this year, I thought it desirable that we should deal with it at this session.

The other amendment has to do with the re-hearing of applications upon the presentation of new evidence, and will be of advantage to a large number of men, although it is difficult to say how many. We know that from day to day representations are being made to us in which it is claimed that the individual, although he has gone to the pension board and the appeal board and failed in .both cases, has been able to find new evidence since, but has been prevented from fifing another application. Upon new evidence being submitted which in the opinion of a majority of the pension board is sufficient, under this amendment a re-hearing will be granted and an appeal from that re-hearing will be permitted if the decision is adverse to the applicant.

May I ask the
minister a question just there? Since he has found the seven year limit to be a failure, why make it nine? Why put any limit on it at all?

I desire to extend that period for two years in order that that situation may be met while we are re-drafting the act next year. The veterans have laid down the principle that a soldier who has a pensionable condition due to war service should have the opportunity to make his representations at any time, which goes much further than anything we have yet considered. There is something to be said for it, however. In order that that situation may be covered for the present, I am suggesting this extension for two years-which has another advantage as well. Those returned men who have failed to file their claim will now have it brought to their attention that they are permitted another two years in which to do so, and they will be more apt to get busy and hand in their claims at once in order that they will have more chance of being considered. The longer these claims run and the older they become, the more difficult it will be for the applicant to prove his case.
I do not think it is necessary for me to continue at greater length. I believe the adoption of the amendments I have suggested and the undertaking of a consolidation of the act next year after thorough consideration and study, when the government will be prepared ito bring down further amendments, will meet the situation. The matter to my mind should be then referred to a special committee of this House early in the session, in order that all the details may be properly surveyed and scrutinized from various angles.

Private Bills
It is easy to say, "amend the Pension Act and reinstate the insurance act." This plan of insurance was adopted right at the close of the war in order to take care of a group of men who were not pensionable; they were given an opportunity of taking insurance and I think that continued until 1922. Some $70,000,000 or $80,000,000 of insurance was written, some of which has lapsed, and from that time until quite recently there has not been any great demand to open up this insurance scheme. We must remember that it is ten years since the close of the war; men who were thirty years of age then are forty today, and the insurance risk is not so good as it then was. Although it might be serviceable to some I am satisfied that it would not be fair for the government to bring in an amendment which would open up the insurance act for another period of years, with the little knowledge they now possess.
I would like to ask the minister a question. Why not deal with that matter at this session?

I think I have concluded the remarks I have to offer, Mr. Speaker. I am satisfied that if these two amendments become law the ex-service men will have been satisfied on two important items.

Hon. CHARLES STEWART (for the Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved
the second reading of Bill No. 269, to amend the Immigration Act.

Mr. Speaker, in my judgment this bill should not be proceeded with. It is a single clause bill, but it is one of great importance. Section I states:
Section 41 of the Immigration Act, chapter 27 of the statutes of 1910, as enacted by chapter 26 of the statutes of 1919, is repealed.
It deals with the power of deportation. It is said that the section will never be put in operation, and therefore it should be repealed. But it is always desirable to have upon the statute books legislation to which an appeal may be made in the event of necessity arising, and the non-use of legislation is sometimes the best reason why it should remain. Not long since in England they had recourse to legislation that was more than one hundred years old, and this statute providing for summary deportation without trial at a time of great stress and strain will not be used except where the conditions obtain to which it has reference. These conditions, let us hope, will very rarely arise in this country, but when they do arise no harm can be done in having here the machinery upon which we can rely and which we may use. Unless some good reason is given why this section should be repealed, it should remain; the fact that it is drastic legislation is not a good reason for its repeal. Legislation which it is said takes away the right of a man to trial by jury and matters of that kind is legislation that sometimes has to be used in all countries for the preservation of law and order, and that is far more important than the possible chance of its application to individuals perhaps once in a hundred years. What harm is being done by having the legislation there? There may arise a condition when it would be profoundly useful to this country. If when that condition arises the legislation is not there, we have no power to deal with the situation. Until it is shown to the House that the legislation will work an injustice in the ordinary course of events it should remain on the statute books. I submit that no reason has been given why it should be dropped at this time, and therefore, and in view of the fact that it is midnight, I move the adjournment of the debate.
